title: John E.Thiel, Now and Forever: A Theological Aesthetics of Time. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 2023, 203pp. $50.00
abstract: John E. Thiel's Now and Forever claims to offer a novel thesis that is said to be rarely discussed in contemporary theology: that heaven is temporal. In Chapter 1, Thiel takes the reader through a discussion of nature and grace, with occasional reflections on Kant and popular physics. The text does not engage with the philosophy of time and contains an abundance of adjectives attached to the word time that leave the question ‘what is time?’ unanswered. To be sure, Thiel does tell us that time is a created dimension of grace, but that does not sufficiently illuminate what time itself is. Readers will come across terms like existential time, tragic time, graced time, fallen time, time now, anomic time, atemporal temporality and serene time. But it is rare that the author moves towards a definition of such terms. In Chapter 2, Thiel discusses the difference between an ‘aesthetics of time’ and an ‘aesthetic of time’. The difference between the two is opaque, but the author emphasizes that he will be offering an aesthetic (instead of an aesthetics) of time. Some readers might find this puzzling since the subtitle of the book is A Theological Aesthetics of Time. Every now and then, Thiel switches back to the word aesthetics, yet the meaning of such usages is unclear. According to Thiel, the payoff from this discussion is that one learns that all time is eschatological time. Chapter 3 purports to move into a discussion of metaphysics, with most of the discussion focused on Chapter 11 from Augustine's Confessions. Thiel promotes the theory that Augustine believes that time is merely a subjective extension of the mind. Though this reading is typically said to be debunked, Thiel supports his reading of Augustine with a quotation from 11.27 wherein Augustine claims that time is not objective. Unfortunately, I was unable to find this quotation in my different translations of the Confessions. After this discussion of Augustine, Thiel moves back to popular physics before declaring that he has developed a new way of understanding God's immanence in the world. Chapter 4 seeks to address the existence of evil in God's graced time. The chapter starts out by asserting that the majority view within Hinduism is Advaita Vedanta wherein all of reality is the illusion of a non-personal deity. According to Thiel, Hinduism feels unthreatened by the tension between the existence of God and the existence of evil. As the chapter progresses, Thiel pushes the critique that theodicies lack moral sensitivity. He also claims that John Hick's ‘best possible world’ theodicy leads to the erasure of time. Chapter 5 aims to examine ‘tradition’ with the category of aesthetics. On page 119, Thiel claims that no one has yet done this. However, in a footnote, he lists several authors who could be considered as exceptions to this rule (for example, David Brown's five-volume series on theological aesthetics). We come to the conclusion in Chapter 6, where Thiel argues for a temporal heaven. Throughout the book, Thiel continually claims that the Christian tradition has tended to affirm a timeless heaven. Though he offers the reader few sources, he does provide some suggestive citations from Aquinas that do seem to imply a timeless heaven. I do not doubt Thiel's reading of Aquinas here. However, I find myself uncertain that the majority view throughout Christian history has been to affirm a timeless heaven. This is because the idea of an ongoing theosis, and other related ideas, are major eschatological themes. In previous publications, I cite people who affirm a timeless heaven, so I know that this position does exist within the Christian tradition. I just do not know how widespread it really is. After all, Amazing Grace sings about how after we have been in heaven for ten thousand years, we have no less days to sing God's praise than when we first begun. All in all, I agree wholeheartedly with Thiel's thesis. I fully affirm the temporality of heaven. I think that this can easily be established on biblical and philosophical grounds. The Bible knows absolutely nothing of timeless existence and speaks of heaven in terms of life everlasting. The philosophical grounds are also quite easy to establish. Part of temporal existence is having a before and after. The afterlife comes after death. But alas, Thiel's book does not give us any transparent arguments of this sort. While the book is lucid in its writing style, there is an insufficient engagement with the relevant literature that leads Thiel to some unfortunate mischaracterizations of various views. For example, one would expect a book that claims to be about the metaphysics of time to interact with at least one book on the metaphysics of time. However, there is no engagement with the philosophy of time in this book. Some readers may find the alleged novelty of Thiel's thesis peculiar since myself and many others have published on the topic of a temporal heaven. One might think of T.F. Torrance's Space, Time, and Resurrection, or John Polkinghorne's The End of the World and the Ends of God: Science and Theology on Eschatology – not to mention the works of Antje Jackelen, N.T. Wright and Keith Ward, or the theological aesthetics of Jeremy Begbie. Another weakness of the book is the consistent mischaracterization of various views. For example, Thiel claims that process theology's emphasis on the present moment distracts from the ways in which the future is latent in the present. This is unfortunate, since process thinkers going all the way back to Whitehead have emphasized the ways in which the present encompasses all that has come before, and how God infuses the present with all future possibilities. Perhaps a deeper engagement with process metaphysics would have prevented this. Thiel's characterization of Hinduism and the problem of evil is also somewhat difficult to make sense of. Belief in a personal monotheistic deity is a very popular view within Indian philosophy, and the problem of evil has been a major topic of debate for centuries. Readers might consider Gavin Flood's Hindu Monotheism for a better understanding of Indian philosophy. From there, I recommend Arthur L. Herman's The Problem of Evil and Indian Thought, and the various entries on Indian philosophy in the Blackwell and Cambridge handbooks on the problem of evil. Overall, the discussion on the problem of evil is somewhat surprising. Recall that Thiel critiques Hick's ‘best possible world’ theodicy, and says that Hick's view leads to the erasure of time. This is a remarkable claim since Hick is critical of Leibnizian best possible world theodicies. Also, it is difficult to figure out how an open theist like Hick who believes in a temporal afterlife can be guilty of erasing time. I would have liked to see some more argument from Thiel to back up these claims. Chapter 6 also contains some random statements that are quite puzzling. On page 171, Thiel says that we should affirm God's ‘omnitemporality’. This is odd since Thiel has continually affirmed divine timelessness throughout the book, and the footnotes chide anyone who dares to affirm divine temporality. Perhaps Thiel is not using the word omnitemporality in the way that it is typically used in debates on God and time. In standard discussions, the term is an affirmation of divine temporality. Again, it seems that an insufficient engagement with the literature has led to some weaknesses in the book.

title: The Problem Field of Christian Theodicy: A Historical Essay
abstract: Проблема теодицеи и размышления на тему зла всегда тревожили умы философов и богословов. Что изменилось с эпохи античности до нашего времени? Можно сказать, что античность, так же как и христианская классическая традиция, не придавали проблеме зла того значения, которое она получила во второй половине ХХ в. Моральный и онтологический аспект зла хотя и вызывал вопросы, но на него можно было смело ответить в духе свт. Василия Великого: реально лишь то зло, которое порождается свободой человеческого выбора. Другие виды зла не есть зло само по себе. После крушения надежд построить новый гуманистический мир, вызванного двумя мировыми войнами, богословы и философы, подражая Готфриду Лейбницу, задумались: живём ли мы в лучшем из возможных миров? Как возможно веровать в Бога, проповедуемого христианами, и допускать присутствие такого количество страданий, учитывая, что Господь наделён всемогуществом и абсолютной благостью? Новое секулярное и во многом дехристианизированное общество не может удовлетвориться ответом в духе святых отцов, где многое решается ссылкой на тайну. Современные люди ставят вопрос более радикально: возможно ли рациональное познание тайны зла и понимание Промысла Бога? Мыслители ХХ и XXI вв. пытаются так ответить на этот вызов, чтобы ответ удовлетворил не только верующих, но и неверующих людей. The problem of theodicy and reflections about evil have always disturbed the minds of philosophers and theologians. What has changed from the era of antiquity to our time? It can be said that antiquity, as well as Christian classical tradition, did not attach to the problem of evil the importance the second half of the 20th century bestowed on it. The moral and ontological aspect of evil, although raised questions, but could be safely answered in the spirit of St. Basil the Great: only the evil generated by the freedom of human choice is real; other kinds of evil are not evil in themselves. After the two world wars caused a collapse of hopes for building a new humanistic world, theologians and philosophers started contemplating in Gottfried Leibniz’s manner: do we live in the best possible world? How is it possible to believe in the God preached by Christians and allow the presence of so much suffering, given that the Lord is endowed with omnipotence and absolute goodness? The new secular and largely de-Christianized society cannot arrange an answer in the spirit of the holy fathers, where much rests on mystery. Modern people pose the question more radically: is it possible to rationally comprehend the mystery of evil and understand the Providence of God? To this challenge, thinkers of the 20th and 21st centuries are trying to find an answer which would satisfy not only religious believers, but also non-believers.

title: Leibniz: an Intellectual Biography. By Maria Rosa Antognazza
abstract: Pp. xxvii, 623 , Cambridge University Press , 2009 , £25.00/$39.95. Antognazza richly fulfils the reader's hope of having received the definitive intellectual biography of Leibniz for our time. She does this by building gratefully upon her predecessors and having worked through the mountain of finished, half-finished, and only roughly sketched projects that this perpetual-motion machine left as his Nachlass in 1716. She has worked through it all, and has pieced together the embryology and probable date of each work she uncovers. Leibniz was a generous listener who enjoyed and depended upon the stimulus of conversation, not to launch his projects but to determine the style, shape, audience and objections to be addressed in each. The vast majority ended up half-finished not because he was lazy, but because he was pursuing so many projects simultaneously. The child is father to the man, and Antognazza is expert at locating the psycho-social origin of Leibniz's life-project in the (broken) condition of the Holy Roman Empire in the wake of the Reformation and 30 Years War. Geography is metaphysics, and central Europe had no literal or intellectual ‘frontier’ to serve as a cultural safety valve into which people who found the pressure too great could escape. Lutheranism, Calvinism, and Catholicism were the three unalterable dispensations that had to be stitched back together again; this defined the intellectual-cultural project that became ‘German Philosophy’ (although Leibniz wrote primarily in Latin and French) with a remarkable consistency from Leibniz to Hegel. Heresy and ‘colonies’ did not exist as options, as they did for residents of the more outlying regions, such as France and England. In fact, there was as yet no ‘Germany’, only a sorry crazy-quilt of independent duchies and principalities derived from ‘cuius region, eius religio’ after the Treaty of Westphalia. German philosophy was conceived ‘after the Fall’ and was playing ‘intellectual catch-up’ from its inception. Leibniz embraced this cultural restitution as a vocation (he speaks of it at one point as his ‘vow’, and never married, or apparently even seriously considered marriage). It will come as a surprise to some to learn that he was first a jurist and counsellor, not a mathematician. He developed his mathematics only during his first visit to Paris when he realized he had to become more rigorous in his mathematics to be taken seriously as a thinker. In the event, he tied his advances in mathematical thinking to his grand project of ‘reform’ and ‘reconciliation’ in all areas, not the least philosophy and theology; this explains the enthusiasm and novelty of the latter, but also their weaknesses. None of the ancients claimed that this was the ‘best’ possible world, that God made the world as a clockmaker, or in the face of apparently insuperable differences proposed ‘let us calculate.’ Much of his thinking was based on the correct insight that different traditions are attached to different words – which, by the ‘identity of indiscernibles’, often have a very near meaning. If we could demonstrate this through a neutral language, the fighting might cease. His grand project from the beginning was not knowledge (or mathematics) for its own sake, but ‘the glory of God and the advancement of the public good by means of useful works and beautiful discoveries.’ Finding new ways to pump water out of the Hartz mines, founding the first journals and scientific societies in Berlin, Vienna, and St. Petersburg, and silkworm cultivation on mulberry trees in Saxony were all part of the same grand project. Antognazza shows how even during his lifetime the vulnerable points of his ‘system’ were identified – for example, the Dutch professor De Volder was ‘baffled’ trying to understand how an immaterial monad could generate our experience of bodies, and the Frenchman Jaquelot claimed that Leibniz's system differed from ‘occasionalism’ only because he stuffed all the soul's ideas into it in advance, whereby they came out in proper succession according to a ‘pre-arranged harmony’. Rather than following Aquinas in taking God out of time entirely (for Whom all moments are ‘perpetually present’), Leibniz preferred to take a ‘phenomenal’ perspective and talk about, for example, God stuffing both the ‘laws of nature’ and ‘miracles’ into the cosmos ‘at the beginning’. This jack-in-the-box approach to Nature intrigued more than it persuaded. Perhaps the deepest problem with his mathematical rhetoric and indefatigable ‘optimism’ was that they inevitably raised the suspicion ‘Methinks he doth protest too much’. Leibniz could not see (as Lessing and Schopenhauer later pointed out) that if we are always making progress but never arriving at our destination, this is equivalent (by the ‘identity of indiscernibles’) to a deep cosmic frustration and provides grounds for pessimism. It is the mirage in the desert constantly receding as we approach it. Leibniz had no sense for the tragic, and tried to outflank evil with mathematics and technology. These two remain the resources for many today in dealing with the evil today, but it is difficult for us to maintain his optimism.

title: مسألة الفعل الإلهي وتعليله بالأغراض بين فلسفة الاعتزال والمدرسة الأشعرية وتجلياتها عند فيلهلم ليبنتز "دراسة تحليلية نقدية مقارنة".
abstract: يعد هذا البحث همزة وصل بين الفكر الإسلامي الأصيل المتمثل في تراث السادة الأشاعرة والمعتزلة، وبين الفلسفة الحديثة المتمثلة في كبار فلاسفة العصر الحديث غوتفريد فيلهلم ليبنتز في معالجة قضية الفعل الإلهي وتعليله بالأغراض. ويدور البحث حول الإجابة عن هذه التساؤلات: هل تُعَلَّل أفعاله تعالى بالحِكَم والمصالح فلا يفعل إلا لعلة؟ وإذا أمكن القول بأن الفعل الإلهي له علة وغاية، فهل معنى ذلك أن العلة هي الموجِبة والملزِمة للفعل أو أنها مرجِّحة وداعية؟ وهل يلزم من نفي الغرض والعلة نفي الحكمة في أفعاله تعالى؟ وهل القول بأن الله خالق كل شيء لحكمة، وأن فعله كله خير، يتعارض مع وجود الشر في الكون؟ فبينما ذهبت المدرسة الاعتزالية إلى وجوب تعليل أفعال الله – تعالى – بالأغراض، نرى المدرسة الأشعرية تنفي التعليل بالغرض. وعلى الطرف الآخر، الناظر في فكر الفيلسوف الألماني فيلهلم ليبنتز يرى أنه دافع عن الفعل الإلهي والعدالة الإلهية من خلال مؤلفه (ثيوديسه) – أي العدالة الإلهية – مؤكدًا على أن الفعل الإلهي فعل تام، وأن العناية والحكمة الإلهية تشمل الكون بأكمله، مما جعل هذا العالم الذي نعيش فيه هو أفضل العوالم الممكنة. وقد استخدم "الثيوديسا" لتفسير علاقة الفعل الإلهي بالشر في العالم. فإن ما يبدو في العالم من آلام وشرور في نظر ليبنتز لا يتنافى مع إله عادل حكيم، والقول بخيرية الله وحكمته وعدله ولا يتعارض مع الكمال العام الكلي الذي يتوافق والانسجام الأزلي الذي يسود هذا العالم. وهذه الفكرة التي صاغها فيلهلم ليبنتز في مفهوم فلسفي "الثيوديسا" أو الحكمة الإلهية هي نفسها ما قال به متكلمو الإسلام – قبل ليبنتز – فقد قرر المعتزلة أن الله لا يفعل إلا الصلاح والخير، ويجب من حيث الحكمة رعاية مصالح العباد، وكل ما في العالم من آلام وشرور هو الأصلح – في نظرهم – حسب الخطة الإلهية لنظام الكون. كما أن نظرية أفضل العوالم الممكنة التي نادى بها ليبنتز قال بها حجة الإسلام الغزالي في عبارته الشهيرة: (ليس في الإمكان أبدع مما كان). هذا، وكان من نتائج البحث أنه على الرغم من وجود تباين في الدوافع والأصول الاعتقادية بين متكلمي الإسلام وبين فيلهلم ليبنتز، إلا أن موقفهم من مسألة الفعل الإلهي كان متشابهًا، مما يدل على أن فلاسفة العصر الحديث – في أكثرية الأمر – مقلدون أو ناقلون للفكر الإسلامي. This study represents a link between authentic Islamic thought, as embodied in the heritage of the Ash‘ari and Mu‘tazilite schools, and modern philosophy as represented by one of the leading philosophers of the modern era, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, in addressing the issue of divine action and its justification by purposes. The research revolves around answering the following questions: Are the acts of God justified by wisdom and benefits, such that He does nothing except for a reason? If it can be said that divine action has a cause and an end, does this mean that the cause is necessary and binding for the action, or is it merely a factor of preference and motivation? Does denying purpose and cause in divine acts necessarily entail denying divine wisdom?And does the claim that God created everything for a wisdom, and that all His acts are good, contradict the existence of evil in the universe?While the Mu‘tazilite school held that God’s acts must be justified by purposes, the Ash‘ari school rejected justification by purpose. On the other hand, the German philosopher Wilhelm Leibniz defended divine action and divine justice in his work Theodicy—that is, Divine Justice—emphasizing that divine action is perfect, and that divine providence and wisdom encompass the entire universe. This led him to assert that the world we live in is the best of all possible worlds. He used “Theodicy” to explain the relationship between divine action and the existence of evil in the world. According to Leibniz, the pains and evils apparent in the world do not conflict with the existence of a just and wise God. Affirming God’s goodness, wisdom, and justice does not contradict the overall perfection and eternal harmony that prevail in this world. This idea, expressed by Leibniz in the philosophical concept of “Theodicy” or divine wisdom, was in fact already articulated by Muslim theologians before him. The Mu‘tazilites held that God does nothing but what is good and beneficial, and that divine wisdom requires consideration of human interests. All the pains and evils in the world are, in their view, ultimately for the best according to the divine plan for the order of the universe. Moreover, the theory of the best possible worlds, advocated by Leibniz, was expressed earlier by Imam al-Ghazali in his famous statement: “There is nothing in possibility better than what exists.” The study concludes that, despite differences in motivations and theological foundations between Muslim theologians and Wilhelm Leibniz, their positions on the issue of divine action were remarkably similar. This indicates that many modern philosophers were, in essence, imitators or transmitters of Islamic thought
venue: Mağallaẗ Kulliyyaẗ Uṣūl Al-Din wa Al-Daʿwah Bil-Munūfiyyāẗ

title: Mind, Value, and Cosmos: On the Relational Nature of Ultimacy
abstract: Humanity has long wondered about the nature of ultimacy. Why does the world exist? What are the necessary conditions for its existence? In the history of Western philosophy, many have proposed answers to such questions. One thinks of Plato's theory of Forms, Hegel's idealism, and—especially for readers of this journal—Whitehead's process metaphysics. Each of these philosophers belongs to what Andrew Davis calls the axianoetic tradition, which upholds the ultimacy of Value (axia) and Mind (noētikos). Axianoetic thinkers thus maintain “that something, and perhaps someone, ultimately mind-like and of immeasurable value” is a necessary notion to explain “the possibility, character, and reason for all existence” (2). This approach to ultimacy inspires Davis's fascinating study in Mind, Value, and Cosmos, which brings Whitehead into conversation with two contemporary idealists: John Leslie, who defends a form of pantheism, and Keith Ward, who argues for a type of panentheism. Through comparative readings of these philosophers’ accounts of ultimacy, Davis develops an axianoetic metaphysics and, utilizing Roland Faber's term, a “transpantheistic” theology. Each of these proposals supports Davis's central thesis that the relationality among multiple ultimates—Mind and Value, Possibility and Actuality, God and World—is the deeper reality of ultimacy.Why might axianoetic accounts of ultimacy be plausible? In part 1 of the book, Davis offers several intriguing answers to this question. In the first place, he argues that human mentality and concern with value are not accidental features of an otherwise mindless and valueless cosmos. Rather, for Davis, these experiential characteristics ought to be understood as intimations of an axianoetic “depth” of reality (45). After all, humans are not exceptions from nature. As naturally evolved creatures, we are what Davis calls “shocking exemplifications” of the cosmos. Our axianoetic character may therefore be interpreted as “a clue to the goings-on of the universe as a whole—its reason, nature, and character” (13).Davis contends that axianoetic thought is further supported by the fact that the universe is “hauntingly balanced or ‘fine-tuned’” for life (25). Whereas neo-Darwinians like Richard Dawkins view evolution as a purposeless process, Davis discerns a cosmic “biocentric imperative” toward greater forms of evolutionary complexity and beauty. In this he draws on Whitehead, who argued that evolution's “upward trend” cannot be explained on the basis of survival alone. For Whitehead, evolution is also driven by the aims to “live well” and to “live better”—or in Davis's words, by “something like the beckoning of Value” (27–28). While some naturalists will be skeptical of these teleological claims, Davis balances plausible arguments for his position with a humble recognition that such issues have to do with profound cosmic mysteries.For many philosophers, the greatest mystery is why something rather than nothing exists. Yet for Davis, “Absolute nothingness is an absolute impossibility” (23). Something necessarily exists, he insists, at least in the form of nonphysical abstractions. Davis thus develops another argument for axianoetic thought by defending the reality of Platonic-like phenomena, including possibilities, mathematical truths, and—crucially—axiological principles. If abstract principles of goodness are eternally real, Davis wonders, might an “ethical requirement” for the existence of a good world also be eternally real? And if so, might this principle be “creatively responsible” for the cosmos (42)?The latter question motivates Leslie's argument for “extreme axiarchism,” which is the view that Value (or the Good) is ultimately explanatory of both Mind and cosmos. For Leslie, the “Creative Supremacy of Value” gives rise to divine Mind, which creates by thinking the best possible worlds into existence. Goodness therefore explains existence, and the world is identical to divine thought. By thus grounding divine necessity in axiology, Leslie avoids positing God as an arbitrary “stop sign of explanation” for the existence of the world (43). While Davis views this aspect of Leslie's position as “ingenious” (54), he rightly challenges the axiarchic notion that Value can do anything without being embedded in a concrete Mind. He also criticizes Leslie's pantheism for negating the values of otherness and relationship between God and world.Davis then turns to Ward's “personal idealism,” which differs from extreme axiarchism by prioritizing Mind over Value and by maintaining “a relational otherness” between divinity and the world (82). Although Ward concurs with Leslie that there is an axiological reason for cosmic existence, he argues that Value needs Mind to gain creative efficacy. And yet, Ward also speculates that Value grounds the “inner necessity” of Mind. While the latter claim resonates with axiarchism, for Davis, it differently implies an “internal relationality between Mind and Value in God.” Might this relationality suggest that neither Mind nor Value are more ultimate, but rather that they mutually require one another? Here Davis utilizes Whitehead's concept of “mutual immanence” to theorize a nonhierarchical mode of relation between Mind and Value. As mutually immanent to one another, “Value eternally procures the existence of Mind,” Davis argues, “and Mind eternally conditions the creative efficacy of Value” (92).Mutual immanence is the conceptual key for Davis's theory of ultimacy, which he unfolds as a Whiteheadian alternative to both Leslie's axiarchism and Ward's idealism. After arguing for the mutuality of Mind and Value in part 2, Davis argues similarly in part 3 for the mutual immanence of Possibility and Actuality. In the final section, Davis defends transpantheism, which affirms the mutual immanence—and transcendence—of God and the World. In each case, Davis argues persuasively that to prioritize any of these metaphysical ultimates is to abstract them from their wider matrix of interrelations. As such, the way in which all ultimates are related through mutual immanence is, in the end, that which is truly ultimate. “The mystery of ultimacy,” Davis concludes, “is the mystery of relationality” (213).With Mind, Value, and Cosmos, Davis has written an immensely impressive book. While he gravitates toward rationalist modes of theological reflection, there is also an apophatic undercurrent in Davis's thought—as evidenced by his emphasis on the mystery of ultimacy and by his suggestion that there may be endless ultimate notions (which echoes Pseudo-Dionysius's claim that there are innumerable divine names). The book might have benefitted from a more explicit engagement with apophatic thought, due to the latter's potential to open corridors of communication with certain postmodernists who are wary of the types of rationalist theology that Davis draws inspiration from. Even so, his constructive engagements with the metaphysics of Whitehead, Ward, and Leslie constitute a major contribution to the movement of process theology. Davis writes with remarkable lucidity, and his argument for a relational theory of ultimacy is compelling. As a work of philosophical theology and process metaphysics, Mind, Value, and Cosmos deserves serious engagement from specialists in these areas of study. Interested general readers will also find much to consider in this intellectually stimulating book.

title: Securing the Nation: Neoliberalism's U.S. Family Values in a Transnational Gendered Economy
abstract: Securing the Nation:Neoliberalism's U.S. Family Values in a Transnational Gendered Economy Rebecca Dingo (bio) The Economy of a Culture in Crisis Shortly after the unethical practices of such corporate giants as Enron, WorldCom, and Global Crossing were exposed by the U.S. media in early 2003, Concerned Women For America (CWA), a conservative right-wing Christian women's organization, published Martha Kleder's article "Values-Based Investing: A Tool for Pro-Family Activists" on the "Culture and Family Institute" portion of their not-for-profit website. 1 Appealing to her audience's fear of the fall of the U.S. economy and capitalism Kleder begins her article by stating, "American capitalism is in crisis" and continues to define this state by using terms such as "broken," "scandal," "shocking," "cheating," and "lying." Kleder employs a rhetoric of crisis that is indicative of many U.S. citizen's late-twentieth-century anxieties about the state of the nation, U.S. culture, and personal desires. She draws upon U.S. nationalism's promises for wealth, democracy, freedom, and individual agency and suggests that these values, like capitalism, are also in crisis. Through practicing what Kleder calls values-based investments, individuals can morally invest in the market and fulfill, for themselves and their community, the values that both U.S. citizenship and contemporary conservative fundamentalist Christianity are purported to provide. Kleder's essay persuades her target audience of other "concerned" right-wing Christian women to consider the intricate relationship between contemporary conservative Christian values, truth, ethics, American nationalism, American culture, and the market. Her timely argument identifies what she suggests is one of the core problems in contemporary American culture: that "Christian values and absolute truth" have been abandoned, resulting in a morality "committed to philosophical relativism, the pure pragmatism" where "ethics is merely the art of staying out of trouble, not the conviction to uphold truth and do what is right."2 In essence, Kleder's rhetoric of crisis appeals to the emotions through taken-for-granted and familiar terms such as truth, responsibility, and family, which she links to contemporary anxieties about the morality of American culture. To assuage this anxiety, Kleder suggests that her audience use their own agency and invest selectively in the market. If one acts morally when investing, then the market will provide the best possible world for the individual, her [End Page 173] or his family, and the nation. Kleder ultimately asks her audience to consider the ethical practices of the companies in which they choose to invest—an ethical concern that I share with many others. Yet, this brief article on the morality of the market communicates much more than the seemingly simple call for individual investors in the global marketplace to choose carefully and responsibly their investment sites. Kleder's article characterizes the rhetorical link between the market, family values, and individual agency. This presumed relationship is persuasive because it builds upon a commonsense belief system of personal intervention that places both individual and national economic security into the hands of each U.S. resident.3 Kleder's essay on the value of moral investing is emblematic of the discursive convergence of market fundamentalism, right-wing Christian fundamentalisms, and neoliberal values that structure the rhetoric of pro-family ethics at the end of the twentieth century.4 Significantly, the majority of contemporary conservative right-wing Christian organizations were established within the mid-1970s and early 1980s. 5 Kleder collapses personal agency, nationalism, and marketplace investing into symbols of faith in God, familial commitment, and dedication to American values. Her article demonstrates the rhetorical slippages between family, nation, and free-market and demarcates the terms and values that thread through the conservative right wing Christian's basic belief system: Faith + Family+ Free-market= Freedom. This belief system is strongly situated in the historical and material circumstances of the late twentieth century. Anxious rhetorics of familial individualism, nationalism, and traditionalism are part of this new neoliberal ideological belief system and cannot be separated from the late-twentieth-century global networks of power. title: Does Democracy Require Metaphysics? A Review of Franklin Gamwell's Religion among We the People
abstract: Democracy, we are constantly reminded, is a fragile undertaking. In the American context, recent years have borne witness to a number of threats to genuine democratic polity, including demagoguery, the undue influence of special interests, and manipulation from big-business—just to name a few of the most obvious challenges. In this sense, the kind of careful thinking regarding the foundational bases of democracy that Franklin Gamwell here undertakes is a welcome project. Whether his specific approach to these matters is successful, however, is another matter.The book, the latest among several in which Gamwell addresses similar issues, is divided into eight essays. But while each essay might be considered a work of its own, the book also follows a certain trajectory that ultimately develops a single coherent argument. In my view the fifth chapter, which works to describe the content and significance of his metaphysical approach, is the heart of the book. Gamwell here argues that democracy requires commitment to a twofold humanitarian ideal: “On the one hand, it should affirm the flourishing of all humans, and on the other, all humans, simply by virtue of being human, should have reason to affirm and thus act on this ideal” (122). Such a humanitarian ideal, moreover, requires a certain metaphysical backing in the strict sense, requiring “critical thought about reality or existence as such, the characteristics or features common to strictly all things” (123).The specific, Whitehead-inspired neoclassical metaphysics that Gamwell has in mind assumes that all human beings have a common, although unconscious, experience of the world. As Gamwell has it, there is a distinction in human experience between explicit and implicit forms of consciousness. Explicit consciousness is clear and requires focused attention, while implicit consciousness occurs in the “dim background” of the mind. The latter is important because, according to Gamwell, it provides the prelinguistic basis for the common experiences of humanity, which are all the same. Specifically, we all live in the same world and experience reality as subjects and before language (134). Gamwell follows Whitehead in dividing this prelinguistic, “primitive stage of discrimination” into a three-fold scheme, “the Whole, That Other, and This-Myself” (134). The Whole is Whitehead's idea of God, taken to be “the eminently temporal individual” whose individuality is “always contingent because what is thereby included depends on contingent realizations in the world” (135). What is more, individual “things” are not ultimately real, but lose their substance when taken away from relations with other things, such that the “final real things are here said to be relativities” (135). In this way, the distinction between divine and worldly actualities is a matter of degree between all-inclusive and fragmentary relativity, respectively.Neoclassical metaphysics thus agrees with Kant that moral theory should be defended in its universal subjectivity; however, it also insists upon teleology. As Whitehead has it, this teleology constitutes a metaphysical good when the “many become one, and are increased by one,” at which point we get “the final real thing or concrete singular” (136). The idea is that the past creates conditions for the forming of unity-in-diversity in the present. The “measure of value a given actuality may realize depends on the ordered diversity it inherits.” So, coming to appreciate Lincoln's Second Inaugural is qualitatively better than listening to a banal political speech, due both to the quality of the speech as well as one's learning that allows for its proper appreciation. Gamwell thus presents a teleological proposition that includes certain duties (137). Specifically, it is the duty of each individual to work for the highest possible level of unity in diversity, or communal and individual flourishing. Human relations and flourishing should be pursued for their own sakes because “this telos creates the best possible world for the divine relativity” (139). In this way, Gamwell's metaphysics implies God and collapses the moral and religious duties to strive for human flourishing. Such reasoning, Gamwell insists, implies that democracy is the best form of government and that basic human rights must be guaranteed (142).With this outline of his metaphysics in view, we are better able to contextualize Gamwell's larger argument. The first four chapters argue that democracy needs to acknowledge, at least implicitly, a metaphysical backing. He begins by taking up the thought of Thomas Jefferson, arguing that freedom of religion and democracy are rightly intertwined. He then moves to discuss the work of David Strauss, whose argument in favor of interpreting the Constitution as a “living document” over/against the claims of originalism Gamwell endorses. Yet Gamwell finds Strauss's argument ultimately incomplete insofar as the latter offers only a hermeneutical and not a political solution to the Constitution. In other words, Strauss tells us how to interpret the Constitution, but says nothing about the grounds upon which we should find it legitimate. Gamwell suggests the initial answer in the notion of popular sovereignty, but extends the answer into the next chapter, where he addresses the thought of Abraham Lincoln. The main idea, here, is that Lincoln's endorsement of the metaphysical language of the Declaration of Independence is a necessary step toward fully legitimizing the Constitution. Note, though, that the recognition must remain implicit on the level of a national constitution, wherein explicit references to religion ought to be omitted.This leads to the fourth chapter, in which Gamwell takes up Jürgen Habermas's account of religion in the public square. Gamwell's central point is that in arguing that religious adherents need to think postmetaphysically to participate in public life, Habermas is ruling out the participation of genuinely religious individuals, because, according to Gamwell, religion is bound to a metaphysical way of thinking. Essentially, despite his efforts at forging a creative alternative, Habermas becomes the same as Rawls (105–6). For his part, Gamwell takes issue with the way that Habermas and Rawls describe religious discourse as somehow immune to public reason. Gamwell suggests, rather, that religious claims in public life ought to be subjected to the same kinds of reasonable processes to which all political statements are subject (110 and after).The sixth and seventh chapters take up the thought of Reinhold Niebuhr and Iris Murdoch, respectively. Regarding the latter, Gamwell considers Murdoch a “reserved friend” to theists because, while not a theist herself, he thinks that her metaphysical argument for religion has great promise. At the same time, however, he finds her nontheistic theory of religion to be problematic because it only takes the traditional theistic arguments about God's eternity seriously; she ought to take process theology into account as well. Gamwell's central complaint about Niebuhr is that his ethic implies classicism, Gamwell's term for forms of thought that offer no positive recommendations within history. Niebuhr's problem, according to Gamwell, is that he fails to distinguish between an ideal to be pursued (in which proper activity is defined in terms of its telos) and an ideal to be illustrated (in which proper activity is defined in terms of its character) (166). By Gamwell's lights, theological reflection can properly identify an ideal to pursue, even if it cannot ultimately illustrate the possibility of the ideal in history.As the reader may gather from the previous paragraphs, this text is not a likely candidate for the undergraduate classroom, although a particular essay might find its way onto an upper-division undergraduate syllabus dealing with a narrow topic. So too, the interested reader may find some essays more engaging and germane than others. The argument that one's dedication to justice implies some metaphysical commitments is an interesting one, taken up elsewhere by Nicholas Wolterstorff, Michael G. Perry, and others. On that score Gamwell makes a contribution. I would additionally recommend the chapter on Lincoln, with its attention to the importance of the Declaration of Independence. So too, although I don't think he fully appreciates the negative ramifications of Niebuhr's account of sin, Gamwell raises some pertinent and interesting questions in chapter 6.The broad sweep of the book, therefore, has its compelling aspects. I don't think that the book works very well as a coherent argument, however. Too much hinges on his ability to provide a compelling metaphysics in chapter 5, in my view the weakest chapter in the book, and I doubt many will be persuaded on that score. One might raise equally valid Humean or Barthian objections to his conception of God, for example—just to mention two possibilities. Indeed, the chapter works to describe his version of neoclassical metaphysics, but provides little by way of compelling argumentation. Similarly, one might question the wisdom of this kind of approach in this time and place. On the one hand, the very mention of the study of metaphysics causes a kind of allergic reaction among many academics in departments of both philosophy and religion. On the other hand, there are very few congregations of believers in the United States, Christian or otherwise, who worship the God that Gamwell posits. That is, Gamwell has a very hard road ahead of him if he is to convince academics or believers (or believing academics) to take up his project. Perhaps this is what makes Gamwell's point interesting. But as a practice in democracy, which requires an agreement among individuals (and preferably the cooperation of institutions) to enact policy and develop virtuous citizens, I think this kind of approach is very unlikely to succeed.

title: Julius Caesar Scaliger, Renaissance Reformer of Aristotelianism: A Study of His Exotericae Exercitationes by Kuni Sakamoto
abstract: Reviewed by: Julius Caesar Scaliger, Renaissance Reformer of Aristotelianism: A Study of His Exotericae Exercitationes by Kuni Sakamoto Andreas Blank Kuni Sakamoto. Julius Caesar Scaliger, Renaissance Reformer of Aristotelianism: A Study of His Exotericae Exercitationes. History of Science and Medicine Library, 54. Medieval and Early Modern Philosophy and Science, 26. Leiden: Brill, 2016. Pp. viii + 213. Paper, $135.00. Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558) was a natural philosopher and literary theorist whose work was widely discussed throughout the second half of the sixteenth and the first half of the seventeenth centuries. After this period, it fell into oblivion, only to be rediscovered during the last three decades or so. His natural philosophy has triggered a series of specialized studies on particular aspects of his thought, especially those aspects that were influential in the development of early modern corpuscularianism. Sakamoto's book goes considerably beyond such fragmentary approaches and presents central strands of Scaliger's most important work in natural philosophy, a thousand-page critique of Girolamo Cardano's De Subtilitate, as a systematically integrated whole. In three chapters, Sakamoto explores issues in Scaliger's thought that have not yet been discussed by contemporary commentators. In chapter 1, Sakamoto gives an interpretation of Scaliger's enigmatic remarks concerning Aristotle's commitment to creation theory and the compatibility of Aristotle's philosophical theology with the doctrine of the Trinity. Here, Sakamoto traces the sources of Scaliger's reinterpretation of Aristotle to the tradition of prisca theologia, which was usually appropriated by Renaissance Platonism. In chapter 2, Sakamoto studies Scaliger's qualified rejection of the theory of a world soul—qualified in the sense that Scaliger takes seriously the task of providing an alternative explication of the sense in which the world is a unity. As it turns out, Scaliger's explication of the unity of the world is connected with another central tenet of his natural philosophy, the theory of a hierarchy of teleologically ordered substantial forms. In chapter 5, Sakamoto delves into Scaliger's philosophical analysis of the Aristotelian conception of celestial intelligences and the Christian theory of angels—as Sakamoto brings to light, no matter how exotic these issues may appear to be, they were a major influence on Johannes Kepler's early cosmology. The remaining four chapters take up issues that have already been the subject of more specialized studies: the idea of the best possible world (chapter 3), the conception of void and place (chapter 4), the theory of the generation of living beings (chapter 6), and the theory of mixture (chapter 7). Although there is inevitably some overlap with what other commentators have written, these chapters offer extensive (and reliable) translations of central passages from Scaliger's difficult text and present a wealth of illuminating co-texts, both from Scaliger's commentaries on ancient botanical works, and from a wide range of medieval and sixteenth-century authors who influenced him or from whose views Scaliger [End Page 543] distanced himself. Most importantly, Sakamoto uncovers a tight net of argumentative connections that Scaliger draws between the theological and cosmological issues discussed in chapters 1–3 and 5 and the issues that belong more specifically to the behavior of natural particulars. Sakamoto's book makes a persuasive argument for the claim that, in spite of the seemingly disorganized nature of the hundreds of separate remarks that constitute the Exotericae Exercitationes, Scaliger's thought shows a high degree of coherence and systematic integration. Perhaps the desire for harmonization is carried too far in Sakamoto's reading of Scaliger's theory of mixture, however. Scaliger offers not just one, but two separate treatments of mixture, and while the first claims that "neither forms nor qualities, which have been deprived of their forms, remain" (148), the second claims that "forms that are actualities become potentialities" (155). Sakamoto reads both passages in the light of Scaliger's claim that substantial forms of mixtures can arise through the "mixture of forms" (153–57), and suggests an analysis of the latter idea as amounting to the claim that the forms that have become potentialities "lose their independent existence" and "are integrated into the superior form" (159). title: Aspects of Divine Foreknowledge
abstract: Voltaire’s elegant sarcasm succeeds in conveying the impression that the theologians’ quarrels are unworthy of a wise man’s attention. Calvinism had swept away the intermediaries between God and man. Once upon a time it had looked upon this purge as the very essence of its task. The saints, ritual, and tradition had been dispensed with. The interesting jewish sect of the sadducees also rejected determinism. Christian theorists were obsessed by the problem and could not leave it alone. St. Augustine presented the church with the ingenious verbal solution called “preterition”: some people were elected by God’ sirresistible grace. Outside orthodoxy, of course, the choices are many. There was, for instance, Melanchthon’s synergism, the collaboration of divine grace and human freedom, which still fails to dispose of the matter of foreknowledge.

title: St. Augustine on divine foreknowledge
abstract: Although recent interpretations of Augustine of Hippo's (354–430 A.D.) teaching on Divine foreknowledge are helpful and sometimes successful on their own terms, they often misunderstand and misrepresent his doctrine. This is because, generally speaking, they lack breadth and a sufficient acknowledgment of the specificities of Augustine's presentation. Either too little of his treatment of praescientia Dei has been studied, or his discussions have been approached without sufficient attention to the discipline of context. To redress the aforementioned imbalances and omissions in the secondary literature, my dissertation analyzes Augustine's major and minor presentations of foreknowledge while paying attention to such matters as his audiences, rhetorical interests, choice of terminology, attempts to balance and integrate distinct intellectual traditions, and important transitions in his own philosophical development. To accomplish my larger goal of elucidating Augustine's overall doctrine, I approach his presentations in chronological order and focus a large portion of my energies on analyzing the structure of his concept of praescientia Dei as it develops over the course of his career. Augustine's teaching, I conclude, is consistent, though developing, and problematic. Consistency is present because throughout the whole of his corpus: (i) he predicates ‘foreknowledge’ of God analogously; (ii) his concept of foreknowledge is anchored in his root understanding of God and is effected by his larger philosophical interests and concerns; and (iii) his major interest in speaking of this concept pertains to elucidating God's relationship with human responsibility. It is also evident that Augustine's notion of praescientia Dei expands over the years. Due to his restructuring of his Christian-Platonism, exploration of trinitarian doctrine, re-thinking of his views on Divine election and predestination, and ever-present apologetic concerns, he comes to identify his concept of Divine foreknowledge more closely with his root concept of God. Finally, Augustine's doctrine is problematic because we find that although his developed concept of praescientia Dei relieves specific tensions and unclarities found in some of his earlier presentations, it implies a determinist-like quality which stands at odds with the teaching found in his foreknowledge-responsiblity paradigm.

title: St. Anselm on Divine Foreknowledge and Future Contingency

title: Divine Foreknowledge and Human Free Will
abstract: This chapter deals with a perennial question in the philosophy of religion: How can divine foreknowledge be reconciled with human freedom? That is, if God knows today what you will choose tomorrow, you necessarily choose as God foreknows. But if your choice happens necessarily, then you are not free. AAA insist that God knows future events and that human beings have free will. Augustine points out that the “necessity” involved in foreknowledge is not the “necessity” that conflicts with free will. Boethius (480–524 CE) adds that God “sees” all events from His perspective in eternity. But Boethius concludes that God foreknows all events because He is going to cause them. Anselm, given his libertarian analysis of free will, holds that God knows future free choices because they are immediately present to His eternity. This motivates an “isotemporal” (four-dimensional, eternalist) view of time on which all times exist equally, and past, present, and future are subjective. Aquinas may or may not be an isotemporalist. As a compatibilist he can embrace Boethius&s;s claim that God knows future events because He intends to cause them.

title: Boethius on Human Freedom and Divine Foreknowledge
abstract: Boethius’ initial question in the Consolation of Philosophy is why God, who orders the natural universe beautifully, would allow human affairs to proceed in a chaotic fashion, even permitting the wicked to trample on the virtuous and go unpunished. Lady Philosophy responds that God governs everything well. What seem to limited human beings to be misfortunes can all be turned to good. This introduces the importance of human free will and a perennial question for Christian philosophers: If God foreknows future choices, can they be free? Human foreknowledge is a sign that the foreknown event does not happen voluntarily. God, being eternal, sees all time as present, and so divine foreknowledge does not impose or indicate any necessity that would conflict with free will. Boethius concludes by expressing theist compatibilism: Even free choices fall under the absolute sovereignty of God.

title: Is Human Freedom Compatible with Divine Foreknowledge?
abstract: If God is omniscient and exhaustive knowledge of the future is possible, then God knows (and in fact knew a long time ago) what we will do in the future. But is this compatible with our future actions being free? I address this question by responding to an argument that claims that these things are incompatible. At the heart of this incompatibility argument is the idea that God’s past beliefs about our future actions are “accidentally necessary”—can’t be changed—and that this necessity transfers to our actions. I consider four main responses to the argument: Brian Davies’ claim that God’s past beliefs about our future actions are properly characterised as beliefs about what we will freely do; Alvin Plantinga’s view—stemming from the work of William of Ockham—that God’s past beliefs about our future actions aren’t wholly about the past and so aren’t accidentally necessary; Trenton Merricks’ idea that our having a choice about God’s past beliefs doesn’t require us to be able to change the past; and Alfred Freddoso’s claim that the accidental necessity of God’s beliefs doesn’t transfer to our actions. My response, like that of Merricks, focuses on the idea that God’s past beliefs are dependent on, and to be explained in terms of, our future actions; rather than vice versa. I support this view by appealing to the idea that God’s foreknowledge is simple (an idea I defend against several William Hasker—inspired objections). I argue that neither God’s beliefs, nor their accidental necessity, should be thought of as a threat to our freedom; and that in any event, the accidental necessity of God’s beliefs isn’t something that can coherently be thought to transfer to our actions. I conclude that God’s past beliefs about our future actions are perfectly compatible with our freedom.

title: Saving Eternity (and Divine Foreknowledge and Free Will): A Reply to Hasker
abstract: William Hasker and I disagree over whether or not appealing to a particular understanding of divine eternity can reconcile divine foreknowledge with libertarian human freedom. Hasker argues that if God had foreknowledge of a particular future choice, that choice cannot be free with libertarian freedom. I hold, to the contrary, that, given a certain theory of time—the view that all times exist equally—it is possible to reconcile divine foreknowledge with libertarian freedom. In a recent article, “Can Eternity be Saved? A Comment on Stump and Rogers”, Hasker makes it clear that one of the fundamental disagreements between us lies in what each of us takes to be required for libertarian free will. In the present paper I outline the version of libertarianism that I find plausible, then explain how a libertarian free choice can be foreknown by God. (I call my approach “Anselmian”, in that it is based on my interpretation of the work of St. Anselm of Canterbury.) Then I will explain why Hasker finds this reconciliation unacceptable since it fails to do justice to what he takes to be required for libertarian freedom. Finally, I will argue that Hasker is wrong to insist upon his analysis of free will.

title: ‘All is Foreseen, and Freedom of Choice is Granted’: A Scotistic Examination of God's Freedom, Divine Foreknowledge and the Arbitrary Use of Power

title: On Divine Foreknowledge. (Part IV of the Concordia) by Luis de Molina
abstract: BOOK REVIEWS 369 On Divine Foreknowledge. (Part IV of the Concordia). By Lms DE MOLINA. Trans. Alfred J. Freddoso. Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1988. Pp. xii +286. $34.95. The contents of the sixteenth century Jesuit theologian Luis de Molina's famous work are specified in its title: Liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis, divina praescientia, providentia, praedestinatione et reprobatione concordia-" The Agreement of Free Choice with the Gifts of Grace, Divine Foreknowledge, Providence, Predestination, and Reprobation ." Part IV, which particularly concerns the Divine Fore· knowledge, is divided into seven " Disputations," 47-53 inclusive. These deal with contingency, the presence of all things to God in eternity, God's knowledge of future contingents (including the role of the Divine Ideas), and especially the reconciliation of freedom and contingency with absolutely certain Divine Foreknowledge and Predeterminations. It is Part IV, especially Disputation 52, which contains Molina's well known teaching about the scientia media, God's "middle knowledge," i.e., eternally between the natural knowledge He has of all things possible and the free or post-volitional (according to our way of conceiving it) knowledge He has of all things actual. More precisely, by middle knowledge God knows, before any exercise of His will, what a created free agent would do in various circumstances, both those which actually will obtain and those which, although possible, will never in fact exist. The objects of such knowledge are situated between what is merely possible and what will simply he at some moment of time. They are possible with a certain hypothetical (ex hypothesi) dependence on both Divine and human free causation. Thus, in comprehending them as they are, God's absolutely necessary and prior knowledge would seem in some way dependent upon what is contingent and even created. Molina's doctrine attempts to overcome the paradox in this. A competent admirer of Molina's position, University of Notre Dame Professor Freddoso is not just a master of the Jesuit's baroque Latin, with its sesquipedalian sentences bristling with spiny technical terms. He also shows himself to be a fine logician (earlier he translated portions of Ockham's Summa Logicae), with an excellent understanding of scholastic theology (in areas such as the Trinity, Christology, and the Eucharist), metaphysics, epistemology, and philosophy of human nature . To make the translated work even more accessible, he has in his introduction briefly treated prior parts of the Concordia as preparing the stage for Part IV, has related Molina's concerns to those of present day philosophers of religion, and has made clear the agreement as well 370 BOOK REVIEWS as the main difference between Molina and his " Banezian " opponents, whose position he summarizes from the 20th century theologian-philosopher , Reginald Garrigou-Lagrange, O.P. In addition, he has graced the translation with helpful footnotes. At times these identify persons mentioned by Molina, some of whom (e.g. Richard of Middleton, William Durandus, Gregory of Rimini, or Didacus de Deza [Hispalensis]) would be less than household names today for a non·medievalist. At other times, Freddoso's notes clearly and succinctly explain items of Catholic doctrine which Molina presupposes or to which he refers. Still again, they reproduce important texts of St. Thomas connected with points Molina is making. And something which I welcomed, Freddoso uses his notes frequently to recall and clarify premises of earlier arguments to which Molina later simply alludes without restatement . The translation itself is from the modern critical edition of the Concordia by Johannes Rabeneck, S.J. (Oniae et Matriti, 1953), which I would like to have seen reproduced on facing pages. Freddoso's version is accurate to the point of being literal. Despite that, however, it is amazingly readable. He does on occasion have difficulty with terms like complexio (which he specially notes on page 10) and ratio: whether to understand them subjectively or objectively-but then, doesn't everyone have the same problem? Again, while one might wonder about sentences as long as nineteen lines (e.g. page 178) , they are in fact the legacy of Molina himself (cf. Disp. 52, n. 19, Rabeneck, p. 346, where the Latin runs 14 lines). Freddoso speaks of Molina's " lumbering " prose. But at the same...

title: A Study of John Martin Fischer’s View Regarding Divine Foreknowledge and Man’s Moral Responsibility
abstract: Summary The possible incompatibility between God’s foreknowledge and the free will of the agent shows that this issue is wide-ranging: if God has infallible knowledge of all of man’s actions before he has performed them, essentially, is there the possibility of the free will of the agent and his choice between alternative actions? According to John Martin Fischer, God, as a person, is absolutely knowledgeable, such that at all times, like t and in all propositions like P, He is completely aware that P will take place in time t; only and only if the proposition P is true at the time of t. Apart from this, God, as a person, in all possible worlds, possesses absolute and universal knowledge. It is clear that in this explanation, the object of God’s fore and essential knowledge has a universal and comprehensive range and, as a result, includes man’s apparently voluntary actions as well. However, wouldn’t such knowledge be inconsistent and contradictory with man’s free will and freedom to act? Reconstructing Fischer’s approach and arranging a notable solution by paying heed to his collection of views and if possible, proving the incompatibility of Divine fore and infallible knowledge with the free will of the moral agent depends on inserting two other premises to his claims regarding God and His fore and universal knowledge. The first is that Fischer believes in our lack of control over the past and more precisely, in the Fixity of the Past Principle and second, according to him, free will and voluntariness of the moral agent is based on the ability to choose and attempt the possibility of an alternative by the person. Regarding the first condition, it is important to note that like Van Inwagen in the Indirect Consequence Argument, Fischer too believes in our lack of control over the past and more precisely, in the Fixity of the Past Principle. According to this view, the past is fixed in the present and is out of our control and as a result, we cannot make changes in its events through our present choices. Therefore, in the event that the performance of a particular act is preceded by a change in a past reality, due to the fixity and establishment of past phenomena, a person would not be able to perform such an action. By accepting the Fixity of the Past Principle, it seems we cannot escape the incompatibility between Divine foreknowledge and the free will of the moral agent. However, in dealing with the second inserted premise, instead of denying the truth value of possible future propositions or the possibility of Divine knowledge over them, he tries to distinguish between two meanings of freedom and in this way, clarifies that in one meaning, freedom necessitates man’s voluntariness in performing or abandoning an act and as a result is a two-way reality and in another meaning, it is only synonymous with freedom in performing an action and is not preceded by man’s control and choice in abandoning an act. According to Fischer’s Frankfurter approach, in some cases there are conditions which do not force a person to perform an act; however, they make abstaining from acting upon them improbable for him and despite all these voluntary factors and from a moral perspective, he is considered responsible. Fischer’s approach, with all its importance in defending free will and moral responsibility and its compatibility with phenomena such as causal necessity and Divine foreknowledge, is faced with two main problems. The first is that in this approach, the interfering Frankfurter essence at the beginning of his interference in the alternative process has not been revised. Therefore, it is still not clear whether we are simply facing an “unreal interferer” whose interference starts as soon as he receives any type of reliable context and sign which indicates the occurrence of choice or an act against the desire and inclination of the interferer or a “conditional interferer” is at work; one who displays physical and even spiritual actions inconsistent with his own inclinations and desires? Another problem is that in the Frankfurter models, the complete and absolute negation of alternatives to the moral agent would result in the lack of his free will and moral responsibility.

title: Augustine’s On Free Choice of the Will
abstract: Abstract This chapter explores Augustine’s account of why we sin and who is to blame for our sinning. The first section sets out Augustine’s core view that we sin due to our free choices and that we are to be blamed for our sinning. The second section looks at Augustine’s proposal for reconciling human freedom and divine foreknowledge. In the third section, the chapter explores Augustine’s reasons for maintaining that God cannot be blamed for our sinning even though he foreknows that we will sin. The fourth section presents Augustine’s reasons for maintaining that it is not necessary that some humans sin. Finally, the fifth section discusses three views concerning the relationship between freedom and divine foreknowledge.

title: Medieval Conceptions of Free Choice
abstract: Abstract The philosophic concept of free choice was debated heavily in medieval philosophy. Philosophers argued over whether or not human freedom is compatible with causation and divine foreknowledge, as questions of theological determinism were contested. A number of approaches to the philosophical problem of theological determinism emerged during this period from Jewish philosophers, such as Gersonides, Maimonides, and Ḥasdai Crescas, reflecting a range of libertarian, compatibilistic and deterministic positions which demonstrate the diversity of views on this issue. A summary of the various arguments of Albo’s Jewish and non-Jewish predecessors and contemporaries contributes to an understanding of Albo’s opinion on this contested topic, and to how he innovatively interprets biblical narratives in a unique way that demonstrates his belief.

title: Glimpsing the Pattern and Salvaging a Semblance of Choice
abstract: This chapter utilizes Min as a touchstone to explore a particularly vexing philosophical question: Can foreknowledge of human events be reconciled with our acting freely in them? Philosophers are divided about how to answer this question. Philosophers who believe in an all-knowing creator God are called monotheists. Monotheists are particularly motivated to reconcile divine foreknowledge with human freedom. One of the more popular reconciliation projects from the history of philosophy relies on the idea that God is an eternal and thus a timeless being. Some skeptics object to Augustine's project because it seemingly requires an odd sort of cause-and-effect relationship. The Wheel of Time television series complicates typical philosophical discussions of freedom and foreknowledge. Things begin well enough with Min's claim that everything she sees comes true eventually, which sets the familiar stage.

title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle
abstract: This paper develops the Baysüngür Philosophical Views (BFG), a metaphysical framework concerning the relationship between divine foreknowledge, temporal human agency, and free will. The framework addresses the apparent tension between the claim that God possesses infallible and timeless knowledge of future events and the claim that human beings nevertheless make genuinely free choices. BFG distinguishes divine knowledge from causal coercion and argues that divine foreknowledge does not, by itself, constitute a causal explanation of human choice. Its central conceptual contribution is the Experience–Choice Cycle, represented as Ht → Dt → St → Ht+1, in which accumulated experience influences deliberation, deliberation leads to choice, and each choice contributes to the agent's subsequent experiential history. The framework further distinguishes decision-space possibility from counterfactual metaphysical possibility and examines the relationship between divine knowledge, causation, temporal ontology, alternative possibilities, and moral responsibility. BFG is compared with Boethian timelessness, classical theism, Islamic philosophical accounts of divine knowledge, compatibilism, incompatibilism, Frankfurt-style theories of responsibility, Molinism, and contemporary theories of time. The paper does not claim to provide a conclusively demonstrated solution to the problem of divine foreknowledge and free will. Rather, it presents BFG as a proposed metaphysical research program whose explanatory adequacy remains open to further analysis.
