title: Pascal’s wager
abstract: Pascal’s wager is a type of theistic argument developed by Blaisé Pascal, a French mathematician of the seventeenth century. There are at least four versions of the wager within Pascal’s posthumously published work, Pensées, each of which is a pragmatic argument. Pragmatic arguments for theism are designed to motivate and support belief even in the absence of strong evidence. They seek to show that theistic belief is permissible, even if one does not think that it is likely that God exists, and then to employ prudential reasons to conclude that one should accept theism. Other theistic arguments – the Ontological Proof or the Cosmological Argument for example - provide epistemic reasons in support of theism: that is, reasons to think that there exists an all-powerful, all-knowing, morally perfect being. According to Pascal, there is good reason to seek to inculcate theistic belief, even if one does not appreciate the evidence in support of theism (see Pascal 1960). The role of the wager, as Pascal conceived it, was to move self-interested individuals towards a perspective in which they could appreciate the evidence for theism. Understood in this way, the wager is not a pragmatic trumping of the epistemic, but a means of bridging the chasm between the pragmatic and the epistemic. The wager has the structure of a gamble, a decision made under uncertainty. Pascal assumed that a person, just by virtue of being in the world, is in a betting situation such that one cannot avoid betting one's life on whether God exists or not. The wager concerning God is forced, one might say, since trying to avoid wagering is tantamount to wagering for one of the alternatives. To wager that God exists is to take steps to inculcate theistic belief. To wager against is to do nothing. Bringing about belief is not an action that one can directly will, but one can take steps to try to bring about belief indirectly. If one wagers on God and believes, then there are two possible outcomes. Either God exists and one may have put oneself in a position to gain an eternity of bliss; or, God does not exist and one loses little, if anything. On the other hand, if one bets against God and wins, one gains little. But, if one loses that wager, the consequences may be dismal. Because the first alternative has an outcome that overwhelms any possible gain attached to nonbelief, the choice is clear, says Pascal, one should wager that God exists.

title: The Ethics of Belief
abstract: Is belief in God when faced with a lack of evidence improper? Evidentialism answers yes. According to Evidentialism, it is impermissible to believe any proposition lacking adequate evidence. Presenting a direct challenge to Evidentialism are pragmatic arguments for theism, which are designed to support belief in the absence of adequate evidence. Interestingly, although overlooked by philosophers, there is a version of Evidentialism compatible with a principled use of pragmatic arguments. In addition to Evidentialism, several moral objections to Pascal's Wager are surveyed and found flawed.

title: Pragmatizam i vjerovanje u Božju opstojnost
abstract: This work is motivated by questions and polemics related to religion and belief in God's existence, and also decision about what to believe and on what basis. It is illustrated the main thesis of pragmatism, a philosophical tradition that originated in the second half of the nineteeth century according to which all the beliefs and theories we posses should serve and be of use in practice and in our daily action and should ensure success and reliability in the field of personal, but also social interests. The first part of this work is is devoted to the pragmatic understanding of the truth by William James, a philosopher that is given credit for its development after he elaborated the idea of Charles Peirce. Peirce asserted that our beliefs are in fact rules for action and James defines true theories as being the best instruments for action because they serve as means to achieve all life satisfaction. The truth, for pragmatists, has the function to lead as to what is the most useful and worthwhile. Conforming to that, pragmatism is turning from rationalism and from searching the objective truth and accepts the plurality of truth. The central part of the work focuses on the issue of rationality of religious beliefs in view of the lack of conclusive and experiential evidence for the existence of God. Even so, it is possible to offer pragmatic arguments in support of theism and their basis is to show and point to the benefit of religious beliefs for practical life. Pascal's Wager and James's Will to Believe are the two most famous theistic pragmatic arguments and they are exposed in this work. In conclusion, there is a connection to fideism, the view that faith is not dependent on proof and personal opinion that the nature of true faith is not necessary linked to rationality and absolute objectivity, but rather to one’s inner feelings and hope.

title: Pragmatik iman anlayışı
abstract: Genellikle kanitsal gerekcelerin/ argumanlarin Tanri’nin varligina inanmak icin en uygun yol oldugu kabul edilmesine ragmen, ayni zamanda bu inanc icin kanitsal olmayan gerekcelerin/ argumanlarin da var oldugu iddia edilmistir. Kanitsal argumanlar (ontolojik, kozmolojik ve tasarim vb.), Tanri’nin var oldugunu kanitlamaya calismaktadir. Bunlar, “Tanri vardir” onermesinin dogrulugunu ortaya koymak amaciyla tasarlandigi icin “dogruluga yonelik” olan argumanlardir. Ancak kanitsal olanlarin aksine kanitsal olmayan argumanlar dogrulugu gostermeye yonelik degildir. Bunlar, daha ziyade dogruluk disindaki gerekceleri on plana cikartirlar. Kanitsal olmayan argumanlardan biri de Tanri’ya inanmanin faydalarini on plana cikarttigi icin “faydaya yonelik” olan pragmatik argumanlardir. Bu argumanlari savunanlara gore, pragmatik argumanlara/ gerekcelere dayanarak Tanri’nin var olduguna inanmak rasyonel ve ahlaki acidan mesrudur. Tanri inanci lehinde bircok farkli pragmatik arguman olmasina karsilik, bunlarin en bilinenleri Pascal’in “Bahis” ve James’in “Inanma Iradesi” tezleridir.Bu calisma, pragmatik temellerden hareketle Tanri inanci lehindeki pragmatik argumanlarin rasyonelligi ve dogasi uzerine yogunlasmaktadir. Bu sekilde o, pragmatik argumanlarin, teistik inancin uygun bir gerekcelendirmesini saglayip saglayamayacagini elestirel olarak incelemektedir.AbstractAlthough it has been generally considered that evidential arguments/ reasons are the only appropriate way for believing that God exists, it has been argued that there are also non-evidential arguments or reasons for believing so. Evidential arguments (such as ontological, cosmological, or design) try to demonstrate that God exists. These arguments are “truth-oriented” because they are intended to show that it is true that God exists. In contrast to evidential arguments, non-evidential arguments are not truth-oriented. Rather, they emphasize other reasons apart from truth. One of nonevidential arguments is pragmatic arguments which are “benefit-oriented” because they focus on the benefits of believing in God. For the proponents of pragmatic arguments, it is rationally and morally permissible to believe that God exists based on pragmatic arguments/ reasons. Although there are various kinds of pragmatic arguments for believing in God, the paradigm examples are exemplified in Pascalian Wager and Jamesian Will to Believe. This study focuses on the nature and rationality of pragmatic arguments for belief in God based on the pragmatic grounds. It also critically examines whether pragmatic arguments can provide a proper justification for a theistic belief.

title: The transformative power of accepting God's love
abstract: Abstract This article develops an account of some of the central features involved on the human side in adopting a richly accepting orientation towards God's love. It then builds a conceptual and empirical argument for the conclusion that accepting God's love can enhance a person's mental health and can indirectly enable a person to cultivate or maintain moral virtues – whether or not God exists. Importantly, the article contends that these transformative benefits are available to both believers and agnostics, and an original secondary data analysis is offered to support this conclusion in the case of agnostics. The article explains how this transformative value of accepting God's love may serve as the basis for a novel pragmatic argument for theistic religious commitment.

title: LIBERTATEA PERSONALĂ ȘI ARGUMENTELE PRUDENŢIALE SAU PRAGMATICE
authors: Ps. lect. univ. dr. Virgiliu Peicu
abstract: Personal Freedom and Prudential or Pragmatic Arguments The study introduces a category of arguments about God’s existence and the belief in Him which is different from the ontological, cosmological and teleological arguments. Called prudential or pragmatic arguments, they may provide powerful reasons for personal faith and freedom. The most wellknown pragmatic arguments were developed by Blaise Pascal (1623-1662) and William James (1842-1910). The arguments developed by Blaise Pascal and William James are prudential or pragmatic because they seek to make a rational decision (primarily praxis, prudence) about the existence or non-existence of God. When they are internalized and believed, they lead to personal freedom (of conscience).
venue: Journal for Freedom of Conscience (Jurnalul Libertății de Conștiință)

title: Cosmological Argument: A Pragmatic Defense
abstract: We formulate a sort of “generic” Cosmological argument, i.e., a Cosmological argument that shares premises (e.g., “contingent, concretely existing entities have a cause”) with numerous versions of the argument. We then defend each of the premises by offering pragmatic arguments for them. We show that an endorsement of each premise will lead to an increase in expected utility; so in the absence of strong evidence that the premises are false, it is rational to endorse them. Therefore, it is rational to endorse the Cosmological argument, and so rational to endorse theism. We then consider possible objections.
venue: European Journal for Philosophy of Religion

title: Religious belief without evidence
abstract: We began this book by considering the evidentialist objection to religious belief. The objection, as you will recall, insists that all beliefs – with religious beliefs as no exception – must enjoy the support of adequate evidence if we are to believe them rationally. Most evidentialists insist that one not only have evidence, but also that one see how and to what degree one's evidence supports the target belief. In the light of this requirement, it is quite plain how the evidentialist's demand is congruent with the natural theologian's practice of forming arguments for God's existence, whose premises and strength of conclusion are evident. In this chapter, we consider two positions that, for differing reasons, do not attempt to meet the evidentialist demand, but reject it. Pascal is famous for thinking that, even if theism cannot be underwritten by so-called proofs for God's existence, belief in God is nevertheless rational on prudential grounds, because of the good ends religious belief brings about. Second, we shall explore a position most famously forwarded by Alvin Plantinga, referred to frequently as “Reformed epistemology”, stemming from the fact that he, and fellow Reformed epistemologists follow John Calvin and Martin Luther's rejection of natural theology. Belief in God, they argue, should be accepted as “properly basic”, without the need for argumentative support. Pragmatic arguments Pascal, to whom the reader has already been introduced, was no stranger to the tradition of natural theology.

title: Preface to this edition
abstract: Richard Gale wrote this book to clarify and assess various influential arguments against and for God's existence. The book's positive role is to contribute to “a more adequate conception of God – a God that will prove a worthy object of worship and obedience, even if the case for believing in his existence is shaky” (p. 3). Accordingly, the book examines some atheological arguments, such as the deductive argument from evil and arguments from divine immutability against divine omniscience and creation. These arguments call for “a more adequate conception of God's nature” than that offered by traditional theism. The book's negative role is to identify the inadequacy of some influential arguments for God's existence, or at least arguments for justifying belief that God exists. These arguments include ontological arguments, cosmological arguments, pragmatic arguments, and arguments from religious experience. None of these arguments fares well, according to Gale, but he avowedly ignores “inductive arguments based on design, beauty, and lawlike regularity and simplicity for the existence of God, as well as those based on evil to show the improbability of his existence” (p. 1). So, he reports: “Since I completely eschewed inductive arguments, no definite conclusion can be drawn regarding the rationality of faith.” Instead, he identifies some blind alleys in the rational pursuit of the issue of God's existence. Gale seems content with the absence of a rational justification for belief that God exists. He reports being inspired by “Hume's Philo,” adding that it is “the sceptical Philo whose spirit imbues my book” (p. 2). Still, Gale acknowledges the influence of Kierkegaard (no skeptic about God's existence). He suggests that the absence of a rational justification for belief that God exists “would be welcomed by a wide range of Kierkegaardian types who completely eschew any attempt to give an ‘objective’ justification of faith.” He adds: “I resonate to their view of faith as a subjective passion that outstrips our reason” (p. 387). Perhaps the problem is not with faith in God, but is with a desired “objective justification of faith.” Gale opposes a case for justification of faith on the basis of religious experiences, on the ground that such experiences are not “cognitive,” that is, “alone would not constitute a basis for our gaining knowledge of some objective reality” (p. 287).

title: Faith and Pragmatic Reasons for Belief
abstract: William James and Blaise Pascal both offered pragmatic arguments for believing in the existence of God. This chapter examines faith and pragmatic reasons, and looks at the role our emotions and passions might legitimately play in religious belief. The seventeenth-century French thinker Pascal agrees that there is not sufficient evidence to justify belief in God on epistemic grounds. Pascal&s;s argument was intended to convince us that the pragmatic reasons for belief in God are overwhelming, but the argument assumes that people can compare some pretty inscrutable expected utilities, and the possibilities seem too complicated for that to be feasible. Pascal thinks of deciding whether believe in the existence of God as a sort of a gamble. The chapter discusses a major objection to Pascal&s;s wager. W. K. Clifford agrees that to act on an ill-founded belief is even worse than to hold the belief but not to act on it.

title: The Realism/Anti‐Realism Debate in Religion
abstract: Abstract This paper sets out issues in the realist/anti‐realist debate in philosophy of religion. These include the existence of God and the meaning of prayer. The paper describes motivations for anti‐realism in religion such as the recognition of conflicting religious claims and a desire for tolerance. It explores instrumentalism and reductionism as possible anti‐realist strategies. Parallels between the debate in religion and the corresponding debate in philosophy of science are used to inform the discussion in the religious sphere. Shared aspects of science and religion feature in a pragmatic argument suggesting that the advantages of realism outweigh those of anti‐realism for religion.

title: Le Pari De Pascal Et Ses Ambigüités
abstract: The author rereads Pascal's Wager in all of its complexities and contradictions, rejecting Manichean readings as being far too schematic. Pascal, through pragmatic argument, attempts to demonstrate the rationality of belief. In thinking that he can direct his (imaginary) conversation partner to faith, Pascal gains some autonomy over Jansenist principles. Inexplicably, Pascal's position seems to contradict his vision of Christianity. First, he shows the libertine that gambling on God is rational. Then he reminds him that, according to the principles of Catholicism, even if he places a wager in favor of the existence of God, his eternal salvation is by no means assured. The wager can end only in disappointment, and indeed it fails to provide substantiated proof. The author explores why Pascal chose to use such an imperfect device.
venue: Symposium A Quarterly Journal in Modern Literatures

title: THE WAGER ARGUMENT
abstract: Traditional arguments for the rationality of religious belief such as the ontological, cosmological, and teleological arguments seek to demonstrate that God exists or to show that God’s existence is probable on the basis of the evidence of the senses. These may be referred to as cognitive arguments since they aim to show that we can know with certainty or probability that God exists. In contrast, the argument known as ‘Pascal’s Wager’ (Pascal 1973: 92-6) aims to show that it is rational to believe in God, through consideration of the potential value of having this belief. Hence, the Wager may be referred to as a pragmatic argument for belief in God. A summary of Pascal’s Wager is as follows. We are faced with a decision about whether or not to believe in God. Since God is conceived as in nite and the human mind is nite, it is impossible for us to assess whether or not God exists. Using our cognitive capacities alone, we cannot make this decision rationally. But the decision is forced. Therefore, we should base our decision on consideration of what possible effect belief (or disbelief) in God will have on our welfare or happiness. At rst glance, it seems we have everything to gain and nothing to lose if we choose to believe in God. For, if God exists and we believe in him, we shall attain great happiness in the afterlife. If God does not exist, and we believe in him, we haven’t lost much. (Momentarily, Pascal will re ne this last step.) On the other hand, if we choose not to believe in God, we shall not attain great happiness under any circumstance. The diagram or ‘matrix’ from Hacking 1972 represents the features of this decision problem.

title: Saints, Heretics, and Atheists
abstract: Abstract This book offers a historical introduction to fundamental questions in the philosophy of religion. It is divided into twenty-five chapters. The first chapter discusses the nature of piety drawing on Plato’s Euthyphro. The next three chapters discuss the nature of evil, free will, foreknowledge, and sin in the context of Augustine’s On Free Choice of Will. Chapter 5 discusses Anslem’s “ontological” argument for the existence of God. Chapter 6 explores Ibn Sina’s account of the nature of the soul and immortality. The next two chapters explore the foundations of religious belief and mysticism in the company of al-Ghazali’s The Rescuer from Error. Chapters 9 through 11 discuss Aquinas’s arguments for the existence of God as well as his account of God’s impersonal and personal attributes. The twelfth chapter explores Marguerite Porete’s account of mystical ascent as well as the doctrines of heaven and hell. Chapter 13 discusses Pascal’s pragmatic argument for belief in the existence of God. Chapters 14 through 16 address Spinoza’s understanding of God, our relationship to God, and the foundations of morality. Chapters 17 through 19 explore the argument from design, the existence of God, deism, and the problem of evil. In chapter 20 Mary Shepherd’s defense of belief in miracles is investigated, while chapter 21 explores Mill’s views on the utility of religion. Finally, chapters 23 through 25 explore the origins of modern morality and the relationship between religion and nihilism in the company of Nietzsche’s On the Genealogy of Morality.

title: Religious Fictionalism and Pascal’s Wager
abstract: Abstract This chapter is a re-examination of Pascal’s famous pragmatic argument (Pascal’s Wager) in support of wagering for God, first introduced in Pensées, Part III, §233. It is, in part, a consideration of whether Pascal is best interpreted as advocating a version of fictionalism about the Christian religion. Although it is ultimately concluded that Pascal should not be interpreted this way, his views are remarkably close to the religious fictionalist’s, and, in a sense, his views may be thought of as a precursor to religious fictionalism. In addition, this chapter is also a consideration of how a contemporary fictionalist might adapt Pascal’s argument. Although the new “factionalist” wager suffers from many of the same problems as Pascal’s original wager, it is not vulnerable to them all. In particular, fictionalists can dodge a thorny problem first raised by Antony Duff in 1986.

title: The Moral Hope Argument
abstract: This essay develops a distinct moral argument for the reasonableness of believing in God (conceived as a perfectly good creator) inspired by the pragmatic argument for “the religious hypothesis” advanced by William James in “The Will to Believe.” It also contextualizes the argument relative to familiar moral arguments, notably those of C.S. Lewis and Kant. Briefly, the argument developed here holds that when facing more than one coherent picture of reality, each of which could be true based on the arguments and evidence but only one of which fulfills the hope that in a fundamental way reality is on the side of moral goodness (what I call “the ethico-religious hope”), a reasonable person could opt to believe in the hope’s fulfillment and live accordingly. Following James’ approach, however, this argument does not imply that others who do not adopt such a picture are necessarily irrational or less rational.

title: William Wainwright on the Rational Assessment of the Christian Worldview: Between Rationalism and Relativism
abstract: MYSTICISM: A STUDY OF ITS NATURE, COGNITIVE VALUE AND MORAL IMPLICATIONS. By William J. Wainwright. Wisconsin: University of Wisconsin Press. 1981. REASON AND THE HEART: A PROLEGOMENA TO A CRITIQUE OF PASSIONAL REASON. By William J. Wainwright. Ithaca and London: Cornell University Press. 1995. PHILOSOPHY OF RELIGION. 2nd edition. By William J. Wainwright. Belmont, CA: Wadsworth Publishing Co. 1998. RELIGION AND MORALITY. By William J. Wainwright. Aldershot, UK: Ashgate. 2005. REASON, REVELATION, AND DEVOTION: INFERENCE AND ARGUMENT IN RELIGION. By William J. Wainwright. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 2016. William Wainwright (1935–2020) is a famous contemporary philosopher of religion who passed away in November 2020. I think this is a great loss for all of us. He has made immense contributions to the analytic philosophy of religion, and together with towering figures like Richard Swinburne, William Alston, and Alvin Plantinga, he has led the way for the resurgence of theistic philosophy in academia. I came to know of his work on mysticism when I was working on my D. Phil. Thesis on the argument from religious experience (ARE) in the late 1980s at Oxford University. Wainwright was one of the earliest proponents of an analytic version of ARE—see his early article (Wainwright 1973a) and then his book Mysticism (Wainwright 1981). According to the reviewers Delmas Lewis and Paul Griffiths, Wainwright's Mysticism “is the first attempt at a systematic and rigorous assessment of mystical experience since the publication of W. Stace's influential Mysticism and Philosophy more than twenty years ago. It is also the first work in English during the period of the critical study mystical experience inaugurated by Richard M. Bucke and William James at the beginning of this century to adequately formulate and extensively discuss the philosophical problems involved in assessing the cognitive value of mystical experience” (Lewis and Griffiths 1984, 293). This recognizes Wainwright's important pioneering work in the study of mysticism and religious experience. My doctoral research heavily relied on Swinburne, who was another early defender of ARE, but Wainwright's work had also inspired me. I also thought that his early article (a very short one) in Ratio effectively defused the naturalistic explanation objection to the ARE (Wainwright 1973b). I later had e-mail interactions with him because I submitted my paper to Faith and Philosophy (at that time, he was the editor). In 2009, we invited him to attend an international conference on the philosophy of religion at Hong Kong Baptist University. I came to meet him personally at the conference. I still remember that after I finished my presentation on how to deal with the problem of religious diversity epistemically, he came forward to me and said, “I am sure this must be the way to deal with this problem.” Wainwright is admirable not only for his rigorous scholarship but also for the breadth of his vision and his broad-mindedness. As a Christian theist, he generously quotes theistic mystics from Hinduism and Islam, and his work on the philosophy of religion truly draws on cross-cultural religious resources, while most other philosophers of religion still focus mainly on the theistic or Christian traditions. He is not prone to make dramatic or exaggerated statements; rather, he has a tendency toward understatement. When he wants to say, “Position A is superior to position B,” more often than not, what he actually says is: “It is not clear that position A is inferior to or less rational than position B.” Quite a few reviewers have noticed his predilection for the use of double negatives. While he has his own convictions about many issues, he holds them irenically and is not dogmatic. He welcomes dialogue between seemingly opposite schools. For example, he was delighted about the dialog between analytic philosophers and continental philosophers. This can be seen from his dialogue with Amesbury: a “thing which has excited me personally, because I've been rooting for it for years, is that there is starting to be more of an interface between title: The Principle of Self-Reliance and the Concept of Spiritual Laws in the Transcendentalism of Ralph Waldo Emerson
abstract: The article analyzes the combination of the concept of spiritual laws and the principle of self-reliance in the philosophy of American transcendentalist R. W. Emerson. This analysis reveals the meaning of such combination and the relationship between freedom of creativity and spiritual laws, culminating in a fusion of individualism and holistic principles in R. W. Emerson's philosophy. In the historical-philosophical aspect, R. W. Emerson's reinterpretation of Neoplatonic and Christian teachings on unity around the one God is examined. His idea of freedom, which is not subject to law but is enabled by the integrity of Being thanks to laws, is analyzed. The author considers the influence of these theses of R. W. Emerson's philosophy on W. James and the relevance of some Jamesian pragmatic arguments regarding faith to explain and justify R. W. Emerson's theories. The article also examines the affinity between R. W. Emerson's ideas and European, in particular H. Bergson's irrationalism. For R. V. Emerson, creativity is the meaning and purpose of life. A person becomes creative through the self-realization of a free personality, but, on the other hand, such self-realization is possible only as a step beyond oneself, the use of one's own energy for the affirmation of super-individual values, as well as on the basis of understanding and observing spiritual laws. This is the key to the growth of a person's creative energy and, accordingly, makes it possible to rely on oneself.

title: آلیات الحجاج فی خطاب موسى الأول فی سفر التثنیة
abstract: يهدف هذا البحث إلى دراسة إحدى تقنيات التداولية وهي الحجاج التداولي، وتزداد أهمية دراستها إذا ما اقترنت بأحد الأنبياء والرسل أولى العزم ومن نزلت عليه التوراة وهو موسى عليه السلام من خلال خطبه الثلاثة الموجودة في سفر التثنية والذي توجه بالحديث فيها إلى بني إسرائيل، وذلك بالاعتماد على المنهج التداولي بوصفه هو المنهج الأنسب لهذا النوع من الدراسات، ويأتي البحث ليكشف عن مفهوم الحجاج وأنواعه وآلياته في الخطاب الأول المنسوب إلى موسى أنموذجًا، داخل سفر التثنية. الكلمات المفتاحية: التداولية - الحجاج - التوراة - موسى Techniques of Pragmatic Argumentation in Moses' first speech in Deuteronomy The mechanisms of pilgrims in the first speech of Moses in the Torah This research aims to study one of the deliberative techniques, which is the pragmatic pilgrims, and the importance of its study increases if it is associated with one of the prophets and messengers, To whom was the Torah revealed, Moses, peace be upon him, through his three sermons found in the book of Deuteronomy, in which he addressed the God of Israel, by relying on On the deliberative approach as it is the most appropriate approach for this type of studies, and the research comes to reveal the concept of pilgrims, its types and mechanisms in Moses' first speech within the Torah.

title: Augustine and William James on the Rationality of Faith
abstract: Augustine and William James both argue that religious faith can be both practical and rational even in the absence of knowledge. Augustine argues that religious faith is trust and that trust is a normal, proper, and even necessary way of believing. Beginning with faith, we then work towards knowledge by means of philosophical contemplation. James’ “The Will to Believe” makes pragmatic arguments for the rationality of faith. Although we do not know (yet) whether God exists, faith is a choice between the risk of believing something false and the risk of not believing something true, and in the absence of convincing evidence we may decide for ourselves which risk we prefer. We may be able to experience God in the future and thereby gain knowledge, yet this may be contingent on our willingness to believe. There are key differences, however. Augustine is a Christian with a neo-Platonic bent, James an empiricist defending the religion of your choice. These differences may be less significant than they first appear. After explaining Augustine and then James I draw out the major points of comparison and contrast and suggest a few reasons their insights might be at least partially synthesized. This is the accepted version of the following article: Mark J. Boone, “Augustine and William James on the Rationality of Faith,” The Heythrop Journal (online edition December 2018), which has been published in final form at [See First URL]. This article may be used for non-commercial purposes in accordance with the Wiley Self-Archiving Policy [See Second URL].

title: Retailing Religion: Business Promotionalism in American Christian Churches in the Twentieth Century
abstract: Evangelist Billy Graham once remarked, "We are selling the greatest product on earth - belief in God - why shouldn't we promote it as effectively as we promote a bar of soap?" His comparison is misleading in its simplicity, since it strikes at the heart of the complex relationship between religion and the modern American marketplace. Retailing Religion examines how American Christian churches in the twentieth century promoted their institutions and messages by adopting modern public relations, advertising, personal sales, and marketing techniques from the secular business community. Retailing Religion develops four principal themes. First, Christian churches in the twentieth century followed the promotional trends of corporate firms with only a slight lag time. Second, this borrowing nurtured the growth of rationalism and individualism in American Christianity, which contributed significantly to the religion's modernization. This transformation was especially pronounced in churches' growing dependence on rational methods and numerical metrics, and in their transition from a producer orientation to a consumer orientation. Third, church promotional efforts increased not the secularization but the pluralization of American Christianity by erecting a platform for cooperation among churches, denominations, and religions. Fourth, church promotionalism fostered an ongoing tension between their sacred mission and their secular methods. Wrestling with this tension, both advocates and critics of church promotion labored throughout the century to develop historical, theological, and pragmatic arguments to defend or denounce the practices. The tension was so complex and often contradictory that some of the strongest advocates for religious retailing were also its biggest critics. The key historical actors in this study are the leading pioneers and practitioners of church promotion: organizations such as the Religious Public Relations Council; experts such as Gaines Dobbins, Philip Kotler, Peter Drucker, and George Barna; pastors such as Robert Schuller, Bill Hybels, and Rick Warren; and critics such as David Wells and Os Guinness. In tracing their adoption, development, implementation, and dissemination of the latest business promotional methods, Retailing Religion provides a broad portrait of American religion's struggle to remain both faithful to the divine and relevant to the world.

title: Beyond “Experimental Philosophy”
abstract: The recent emergence of “experimental philosophy” has led to interesting and useful discussions on the sources of philosophical knowledge and its relationship to empirical knowledge. However, the type of empirical knowledge referred to as “experimental” is often surprisingly narrow, and there is a need to widen the discussion to other types of empirical knowledge. Generally, they design surveys to test laypersons' intuitive judgments about philosophical issues, they run the surveys, and they statistically analyze the results. But whereas the “experimental” part of the name refers to the fact that they run studies and collect data concerning folk intuitions, the “philosophy” part refers to the fact that they discuss the various implications these data have for philosophical debates. (Nadelhoffer and Nahmias, 2007, pp. 124–125) … in a typical study, a participant is provided with some hypothetical scenario and asked to decide whether some particular term applies to an event in the story or whether some relation holds. Some surveys aim to determine the variables that influence responses, but other studies simply poll opinions as if the philosophers worked for Gallup. (Rose and Danks, 2013, p. 523) The use of the term “experimental” for the collection of survey data is severely misleading. At least since William Stanley Jevons's classic statement in 1874, scientists and philosophers of science reserve the term “experiment” for those empirical observations in which some object of study is subjected to interventions (manipulations) that aim at obtaining a predictable outcome or at least predictable aspects of the outcome (Jevons, [1874] 1920, p. 416; see also John Stuart Mill's much earlier expression of the same distinction, Mill, [1843] 1974, pp. 392–393). The distinction between experimental and non-experimental observations is epistemologically foundational, and there is no reason to blur it by using “experimental” as a synonym of “empirical”. Terminological issues aside, the use of surveys to identify philosophical intuitions appears to be based on a specific view of what philosophers mean (or should mean) when they refer to intuitions as the source of philosophical knowledge or standpoints. If by intuitions we mean spontaneous, unimproved reactions, then surveys may be an adequate method to find out what people's intuitions are. But arguably, what philosophers call intuitions are often views and standpoints that have been developed and adjusted in discussions with others, thus representing a reflective equilibrium rather than a pre-reflective standpoint. To find out what people's intuitions are in this latter sense of the word, other types of studies are needed, including experimental studies comparing groups that are given access to different types of facts and arguments. But as pointed out by Rose and Danks (2013), intuitions, even in this wider sense, cover only a small part of the information from psychology and cognitive science that philosophers can have use for. We need to know more generally how people think, feel, and decide, and how all this relates to their behaviour. But it does not end there. Cognitive science is only one of many disciplines that philosophers can learn from. Philosophy of time needs to be thoroughly informed by physics, philosophy of language by linguistics, political philosophy by social and in particular political science, philosophical aesthetics by empirical studies of the arts, etc. Philosophy has the potential for fruitful co-operations with virtually all the other academic disciplines (Hansson, 1999). Studies of beliefs about free will provide us with useful illustrations of the difficulties involved in drawing philosophical conclusions from empirical data about folk intuitions. There is empirical evidence showing that most people conceive free will as freedom from internal or external constraints. (Monroe and Malle, 2010) Such a concept of free will is easily reconciled with determinism. However, no amount of data about folk intuitions can exclude the possibility that there is another meaningful but less obvious sense of the term that may be fundamental for our understanding of ourselves but does not allow for compatibilism. Several studies indicate that belief in free will may have significant positive effects, such as a reduced tendency to cheat (Vohs and Schooler, 2008), better work performance (Stillman et al., 2010), decreased aggression and increased helpfulness (Baumeister et al., 2009). It might be tempting to use these results as pragmatic arguments for belief in free will. However, such an argumentation would bring us to a slippery slope that can take us to where we do not want to go. What should we do with the evidence that belief in a punishing God (contrary to belief in a benevolent God) dissuades believers from cheating and promotes what is commonly conceived as moral behaviour? (Shariff and Norenzayan, 2011) And how should we react to the evidence indicating that training in moral reasoning may promote immoral behaviour by making rationalizations for such behaviour more accessible (Valdesolo and DeSteno, 2008; Mercier, 2011)? As so often, new empirical data give rise to new philosophical issues. Philosophy needs to be enriched with much more empirical data. But for the most part, others are much better qualified than philosophers to assemble that data. Philosophy, on its side, has access to a range of useful methodologies that are specific for our discipline. It seems to be a good idea to focus on doing that which we can do better than others rather than that which others do better than we.

title: A APLICAÇÃO DA LEI DE NEWCOMB-BENFORD NA DETECÇÃO DE ANOMALIAS EM CONTRATAÇÕES PÚBLICAS DO ESTADO DO RIO DE JANEIRO
abstract: Este estudo se refere à aplicação da Lei de Newcomb-Benford à detecção de anomalias nas despesas contratuais do Poder Executivo do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (2021–2026), abrangendo 51.185 registros, R$ 170,7 bilhões, 107 órgãos e 40.130 processos, extraídos de portais oficiais. Por sua vez, a metodologia utilizada combinou quatro testes complementares – primeiro dígito, segundo dígito, segunda ordem em análise dual (por frequência e por valor monetário) e Z-score segmentado por órgão – com métricas de qui-quadrado, MAD e Curva ABC, em que se obtiveram resultados de conformidade global satisfatória, superior à observada na literatura nacional sobre entes subnacionais, coexistindo, porém, com anomalias localizadas: o excesso do segundo dígito zero e a presença de valores arrendondados sistematicamente, além de anomalias de duplicação e concentração em órgãos específicos. Com isso, a principal contribuição metodológica foi a análise dual de segunda ordem, na qual se demonstrou serem distintos os pares anômalos por valor (12, 10, 28) e por frequência (30, 60, 50). Por fim, concluiu-se que a técnica constitui protocolo replicável de triagem estatística para os órgãos de controles externo e interno, exigindo verificação documental a fim de se confirmarem as inconsistências levantadas.

title: Small Mammal Live-Trapping Surveys 1992 - 2025, Adirondack Long-Term Ecological Monitoring Program Project No. 24 by the Adirondack Ecological Center of the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, Newcomb, New York.
abstract: Small mammals play an important function in forested ecosystems; they are key predators of seeds and invertebrates, food sources for larger predators, and act as disease vectors. Our objectives in this mark-recapture study are to document small mammal abundance and population changes in managed and unmanaged forests at SUNY ESF’s Huntington Wildlife Forest (HWF). We sampled five sites from 1992-2025 (sampling ongoing). Sites were sampled each year unless disrupted by weather (most notably a flood in 2023 prevented trapping) or non-target animals such as bears or racoons. We trapped for 3-5 nights per site (49 traps per site) and checked traps each morning. We identified, ear-tagged, sexed, weighed, and checked for reproductive condition for captured small mammals, which were then released onsite. Between 1992 and 2025, we captured 16 different species and a total of 8,447 individual small mammals. Deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus) had the highest number of captures (2,976; 974 female to 964 male, the rest unknown or left blank), followed by the Eastern chipmunk (Tamias striatus) (2,372; 480 female to 662 male) and short-tailed shrew (Blarina brevicauda) (1,081).

title: Review of Timothy Bowers Vasko, Making All the World America: Native Information and the Doctrine of Discovery (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2026)
abstract: Steven T. Newcomb reviews Timothy Bowers Vasko's Making All the World America: Native Information and the Doctrine of Discovery (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2026). Vasko argues that the Doctrine of Discovery worked not through the suppression of Indigenous peoples but through European recognition of Indigenous rights and sovereignty, incorporating Native peoples as religious, political, and property-owning subjects. Newcomb finds this reading inaccurate and incomplete. Applying his "domination translator," he shows that Vasko's key terms—dominium, dominion, sovereignty, empire, incorporation—all resolve into the Christian European claim of a right of domination over non-Christian nations. The review faults Vasko for omitting an etymology of dominium, for passing over the explicit language of domination in the papal bulls of 1452, 1455, and 1493, and for misstating the Vatican's March 2023 statement as a repudiation of those bulls. Newcomb concludes that "discovery" is not the issue; the continuing claim of a right of domination is.

title: Pascal's Hell
abstract: ABSTRACT Expected utility maximization with unbounded utilities implies that tiny probabilities of huge positive or negative payoffs can dominate overall expected‐utility calculations. In other words, it leads to fanaticism . Fanaticism is counterintuitive, as illustrated by cases such as Pascal's Mugging and the St. Petersburg paradox. However, these cases do not illustrate the most counterintuitive implications of fanaticism. This paper shows, in the form of a dialogue, how a world filled with fanatical agents can be almost certain to be devoid of value—and by their own choice. The case presented here does not involve infinities, and it avoids the criticisms that have been raised against earlier cases.

title: Sacralizing Dominion: The Doctrine of Christian Discovery and the Religious Nationalist Imagination
abstract: White Christian nationalism presents itself as restoration—of a Christian nation, a moral order, a rightful hierarchy. This article argues that what it restores is the world-making rhetoric of the Doctrine of Christian Discovery (DoCD). Reading the fifteenth-century papal bulls, their sedimentation into United States law, culture, religion, and contemporary dominionist discourse as a single rhetorical formation, we show that the bulls’ vocabulary of discovery, vacancy, and civilization did not describe a world but constituted one: a moral-legal order in which Christian identity conferred sovereignty and racialized peoples appeared as obstacles to salvation and property. That order persists as hegemonic common sense, carried by legal precedent, curricula, and popular culture, and it is re-performed today in the territorial rhetoric of the New Apostolic Reformation and white Christian nationalism. Following Steven T. Newcomb (Shawnee/Lenape), repudiating the doctrine’s documents without dismantling its embeddedness within language and cognition leaves religious nationalism’s deepest resource intact. Against the discovery template, we set three counter-rhetorics—Indigenous theologies, Black theology, and womanism—and argue that desanctifying dominion requires conciliation, not reconciliation.

title: DCHPS Estágio A: estatuto científico, limites de validação e resultados do equilíbrio cilíndrico
abstract: Artigo I — Adendo de correção: estatuto científico do protótipo DCHPS. O que pode ser proposto e o que pode ser validadoArtigo II — Nota de resultados do Estágio A: mapa funcional do artefacto e corte do cilindro periódico O pacote reúne um adendo de estatuto e uma nota de resultados do Estágio A do protótipo cilíndrico DCHPS. Não é tese nova e não reabre o veredicto do artigo-mãe: \(B_{\text{arquitectura}}=1\) com restrições e \(B_{\text{hipótese}}\) como resultado \(=0\). O DCHPS, neste ciclo, é artefacto computacional (integrador de equilíbrio + proxy de tearing + livro de recusa), não máquina física com cadeia de potência.O adendo substitui formulações anteriores por correções obrigatórias (C1–C8): «motor» lê-se solver; «pré-singular» é nome de intenção, não regime medido; \(\Delta'<0\) e \(\gamma_0=0\) são baseline de controlo, não êxito do mecanismo helicoidal; só o balanço radial entra no executável; V6C cinemático e \(G_{DCHPS}\) com \(\Delta P_{\text{fus}}\) estão fora desta corrida. Hipótese científica, aqui, é só o enunciado falsificável por residual declarado antes da corrida no objecto que o código resolve. Ficam H-A (equilíbrio), H-B (proxy Newcomb do modo (2,1), CONDITIONAL a benchmark), H-C (candidato \(F_{DCHPS}=J_{CD,h}\times B+O(\varepsilon^2)\), ainda não testável) e H-D (varredura \(\gamma(\varepsilon)\) com \(\gamma_0>0\), bloqueada enquanto o único equilíbrio publicado tiver \(\gamma_0=0\)).A nota reporta o estado numérico correspondente. Com \(q(0)=1{,}1\), \(q(a)=3{,}5\), \(R/a=4\) e malha de 401 pontos, a integração da pressão no cilindro periódico fecha com residual normalizado \(R_{GS}=\max|\mathrm{res}|/\max|\nabla p|=3{,}96\times10^{-5}\) e \(\beta_0=0{,}021\). A superfície \(q=2\) está em \(r_s/a\approx0{,}61\); o proxy Newcomb reduzido dá \(\Delta'\approx-17<0\), logo \(\gamma_0=0\) no scaling FKR. O termo \(F_{DCHPS}\) não entra (\(\varepsilon=0\), \(P_{\text{abs}}=0\)). As duas figuras (mapa funcional e corte transversal) tornam visível o mesmo facto: o núcleo resolvido é a ODE de equilíbrio; o conector de current drive helicoidal está desligado.Validar, neste ciclo, não é «provar a natureza». H-A conta como consistência numérica; H-B conta só como indicativo; livro energético, mecanismo \(F_{DCHPS}\) e alteração favorável de \(\gamma\) não se validam hoje. O programa autorizado fica em P0–P5 (manter os textos juntos; benchmark de \(\Delta'\); alvo com \(\Delta'>0\); ligar \(J_{CD,h}\) a \(P_{\text{abs}}\); só então varrer \(\varepsilon\)). Nenhum resultado experimental de fusão, de propulsão ou de estabilidade de máquina é reivindicado.

title: Sign structure and entrainment of tearing-mode triads on a relaxed pinch — reproduction code
abstract: Sign structure and entrainment of tearing-mode triads on a relaxed pinch — reproduction codeMATLAB code reproducing every table and figure of> **Paper I — Three-Wave Couplings on a Force-Free Relaxed State: Sign> Uniformity, an Affine Phase Manifold, and a Gauge-Invariant Observable**>> **Paper II — Driven Entrainment on a Force-Free Relaxed State: Amplitude> Closure, a Reachability Bound, and the Ceiling Set by Island Overlap**>> Oleg Agamalov, DSc — Independent Researcher, Pivdennoukrainsk, Ukraine> ORCID [0000-0002-0330-8268](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0330-8268)One archive serves both papers, because they share one equilibrium and one setof Newcomb eigenfunctions and it would be misleading to ship two copies thatcould drift apart. Paper I is the theory: the equilibrium, the three-wavecoefficient, the sign proposition and the closure phase. Paper II is thedriven problem: the amplitude closure, the reachability bound, the device scanand the limits. Every script below says which paper and which section itbelongs to.Base MATLAB only — no toolboxes — and it runs unchanged under GNU Octave 7or later. `fsolve` is replaced by a damped Levenberg–Marquardt solver writtenout in `lib/sasr_newton.m`; nothing else in the archive needs anything beyond`ode45`, `fzero` and `besselj`.Quick start```matlabsetenv('SASR_HEADLESS', '1') % optional: save the PNGs, open no windowsrun_all````run_all.m` adds `lib/` to the path itself and executes the twenty-four scripts inthe order the two manuscripts use them. Every script is independent of theothers, so any single result can be reproduced on its own:```matlabaddpath libs06_locked_branch % Paper II Table 2 and Figure 1, on their own```Figures are written as PNGs into `figures/`, at the same time as they are openedon screen. abstract: Sign structure and entrainment of tearing-mode triads on a relaxed pinch — reproduction codeMATLAB code reproducing every table and figure of> **Paper I — Three-Wave Couplings on a Force-Free Relaxed State: Sign> Uniformity, an Affine Phase Manifold, and a Gauge-Invariant Observable**>> **Paper II — Driven Entrainment on a Force-Free Relaxed State: Amplitude> Closure, a Reachability Bound, and the Ceiling Set by Island Overlap**>> Oleg Agamalov, DSc — Independent Researcher, Pivdennoukrainsk, Ukraine> ORCID [0000-0002-0330-8268](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0330-8268)One archive serves both papers, because they share one equilibrium and one setof Newcomb eigenfunctions and it would be misleading to ship two copies thatcould drift apart. Paper I is the theory: the equilibrium, the three-wavecoefficient, the sign proposition and the closure phase. Paper II is thedriven problem: the amplitude closure, the reachability bound, the device scanand the limits. Every script below says which paper and which section itbelongs to.Base MATLAB only — no toolboxes — and it runs unchanged under GNU Octave 7or later. `fsolve` is replaced by a damped Levenberg–Marquardt solver writtenout in `lib/sasr_newton.m`; nothing else in the archive needs anything beyond`ode45`, `fzero` and `besselj`.Quick start```matlabsetenv('SASR_HEADLESS', '1') % optional: save the PNGs, open no windowsrun_all````run_all.m` adds `lib/` to the path itself and executes the twenty-four scripts inthe order the two manuscripts use them. Every script is independent of theothers, so any single result can be reproduced on its own:```matlabaddpath libs06_locked_branch % Paper II Table 2 and Figure 1, on their own```Figures are written as PNGs into `figures/`, at the same time as they are openedon screen. The file name carries the paper and the figure number:`figure_p1_02_branch_scan.png` is Figure 2 of Paper I.What produces whatScript Paper Section Produces`s01_equilibrium` I 2 Table 1 — q-window, force-free residual, Δ′r_s at eight surfaces`s02_suydam` I 2.4 Table 2 — Suydam pressure limit at each surface, and the same limit along the Taylor branch`s03_selection_rules` I 3 mediant theorem, the detuning identity (13), affine family, V_ijk and its grid convergence`s20_mediant_geometry` I 3.2, 4.1 Figure 1 — the mediant ordering and the two branches at r₃`s04_branch_scan` I 4.2 Table 3, Figure 2 — sign of V_ijk across λa = 1.0–2.3`s05_ideal_kink` I 4.2 the ideal-kink threshold λa = 1.8346`s17_ordering` I 4.5 Figure 3 — how far the guide-field ordering is stretched; (10) term by term`s13_closure_test` I 5 / II 4.2 Table 6 and Figure 6 of Paper II — power of the closure-phase test`s06_locked_branch` II 2.3–2.5 Table 2, Figure 1 — folds of (6), shielding criterion`s07_hysteresis` II 2.4 Figure 2 — hysteresis by direct integration of (1)–(2)`s19_layer_width` II 2.6 what w₀ is; sensitivity of the thresholds and of criterion (7)`s08_network` II 3.2 Table 3, Figure 3 — which triads transmit; the closure`s09_cascade` II 3.2–3.4 Figures 4 and 5 — geometric shielding, the staircase, the gateway`s10_existence` II 3.3 is the closure attained? multi-start scan; the triadic/direct drive ratio`s21_jacobian` II 3.6 spectrum of the linearised closure: are the entrained states attractors?`s22_rotation_shear` I 5.3 / II 6.2 differential rotation against the closure phase: the cancellation, and the locking bandwidth`s23_sideband_sign` I 4.4 / II App. C.5 sign of the toroidal sideband couplings ψ_i(r_j)ψ_j(r_i), over four cut-offs in n`s11_amplitudes` II 3.5 Table 4 — resonant field b_r/B₀ at the surface and at the wall`s12_bridges` II 3.7 Table 5 — toroidal sidebands linking the core`s14_device` I 5.4 / II 4.4–4.5 Table 5 of Paper I, Tables 7 and 8 and Figure 7 of Paper II — RFX-mod2 compatibility and the tearing index of each triad member`s15_shear_chirikov` II 5.2–5.3 Tables 9 and 10 — the shear lever, island overlap`s18_overlap_in_state` II 5.3 Table 10 — Chirikov overlap from the solved island widths`s24_overlap_onset` II 5.3 at what applied field the islands stop being separate, against the gateway threshold`s16_prs` I 2.4 / II 5.4 Table 11 — largest β of partially relaxed profiles, their rational surfaces, and the cautionary steep-λ caseThe script numbers are historical and no longer run in order; `run_all` executesthem in the order the papers do, which is the order of the table above.`lib/` holds the shared machinery: the Bessel-model equilibrium (`sasr_q`,`sasr_geom`), the Newcomb equation and its two-sided shooting (`sasr_nrhs`,`sasr_shoot`, `sasr_dprime`), the three-wave coupling (`sasr_vijk`), thecomplex-flux closure (`sasr_branch`, `sasr_folds`, `sasr_netresid` for thescaled steady-state residual and `sasr_netrhs` for the unscaled dynamics), thereachability closure (`sasr_closure`), and the partially relaxed states(`sasr_prs`).`EXPECTED_OUTPUT.txt` is the complete console output of one `run_all`, so anynumber in either paper can be checked against it without running anything.`figures/` ships the ten PNGs the scripts produce; a run overwrites them.RuntimeAbout half an hour end to end under Octave 8.4 on a single core, and about aminute in MATLAB — the difference is interpreter overhead per ODE right-hand-sidecall, not algorithm. Four scripts account for nearly all of the Octave time:`s04_branch_scan` — 335 Newcomb eigenfunctions across the Taylor branch`s07_hysteresis` — a stiff sweep, 90 integrations at Ωτ_R ≈ 10⁴`s10_existence` — a multi-start fixed-point scan over 110 coupling strengths`s17_ordering` — the coupling evaluated term by term at seven points on the branch`s23_sideband_sign` — Newcomb eigenfunctions for every sideband pair up to n = 20Lower `NG` in `s10_existence.m` or `NH` in `s07_hysteresis.m` for a quicker look,but note that the four-surface state at h = 40 exists over a narrow band in thecoupling and a coarse `g`-grid steps over it.Running under MATLAB on WindowsTested under MATLAB R2018b as well as Octave 8.4. Octave accepts a superset ofMATLAB's syntax, so code developed in Octave can fail in MATLAB and not the otherway round. Two such constructs were found and fixed, and both stopped `run_all`outright:A warning identifier containing a hyphen. MATLAB rejects it with a harderror, not a warning; Octave's identifiers all contain hyphens(`Octave:singular-matrix`). `lib/sasr_newton.m` now selects the id set with`exist('OCTAVE_VERSION','builtin')` and wraps each call in try/catch.Indexing into the result of a function call. `sasr_params().OMPHI` is legalin Octave and an error in MATLAB ("Functions cannot be indexed using {} or .indexing"). Bind the struct to a name first.A third trap is not a syntax difference but a path one, and it is worth namingbecause the symptom misleads. Do not unzip this archive inside the MATLABinstallation tree (`C:\Program Files\MATLAB\R2018b\WORK\...` and the like).MATLAB caches directory listings for folders under matlabroot, so a libraryfunction that is new since that cache was built stays invisible even after`addpath` — and because `run_all` invokes each script by explicit path, everyscript runs normally until one of them calls the missing function. `run_all` nowcalls `rehash` after `addpath` to clear it; `rehash toolboxcache` clears it byhand. Keeping the archive in an ordinary user folder avoids the whole question,and is better practice anyway, since these scripts write PNGs and `.mat` filesinto `figures/`.If you edit anything here, the rest of the checklist is: no bare `printf`, no`endfor`/`endif`/`endfunction`, no `!` for negation, no `#` comments, no `+=` or`++`, and no double-quoted strings. The archive was swept for all of these and isclean; a change is most usefully tested by running `run_all` in MATLAB, sinceOctave will not catch this class of problem.Three things worth knowing before reading the numbersThe normalisation of the inner Newcomb solution is not cosmetic. Startedfrom ψ = r^m with m = 14, the axis solution is of order 10⁻⁵⁶ at the matchinglayer, the integrator's absolute tolerance swamps it, and Δ′ comes out with thewrong sign — +605 instead of −27.8 in the case that first exposed this.`lib/sasr_shoot.m` starts from ψ(r₀) = 1 instead.The sign of the slip term is not a convention. Writing dφ/dt = −Ω instead of+Ω inverts the stability condition of Paper II Section 2.5, so that onlytearing-unstable surfaces can lock. That is a spurious result which reproducesplausible-looking hysteresis loops and is caught only by the linearisation, or bynoticing that a locked surface has Ω exceeding its unforced value.The residual the solver minimises is not the right-hand side. `sasr_netresid`rescales each block so that a surface carrying ψ ~ 10⁻¹² counts in the normalongside a penetrated one — without it the solver reports success while theshielded surfaces are still wrong. That rescaling also changes the Jacobian, sothe stability calculation in `s21_jacobian` uses `sasr_netrhs`, which is theunscaled dynamics of (1)–(2), and re-verifies the fixed point there before takinga spectrum.Unconverged solves are discarded, never carried forward. In `s10_existence`a solve returning a scaled residual of 10⁻¹⁰ or worse is thrown away. An earlierversion of that calculation carried such states forward — 110 of 161continuation steps, with residuals up to 2×10⁶ — and produced a headline resultthat did not survive audit. The number of rejected solves is printed so thereader can see how much of the coupling range simply has no fixed point.Where this archive and the manuscripts differThe manuscripts were corrected against this archive, so the three now agree onevery number that appears in a table. What remains are two conventions and oneirreducible difference.The symbol F means two things, and Paper I says so

title: Urobiome, urinalysis, sample classification, and Bray–Curtis data from 211 urine samples contributed by 92 asymptomatic adults with spinal cord injury or disease using intermittent catheterization
abstract: Data underlying Tractenberg RE, Groah SL, Newcomb E, Khemmani M, Joyce C, Wolfe AJ, Riegner CR. Variation in urobiome composition over time in asymptomatic individuals with spinal cord injury and disease using intermittent catheterization. PLOS ONE (2026). Adults with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction due to spinal cord injury or disease, all using intermittent catheterization, each contributed one to four urine samples collected while asymptomatic and at least two weeks apart. Samples were characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, urinalysis, standard urine culture, and the Urinary Symptom Questionnaire for Neuropathic Bladder–Intermittent Catheter version (USQNB-IC). Files - S1_File_participants.csv — one row per participant (n = 92). - S2_File_samples.csv — one row per sequenced sample (n = 224; the 211 analysed are flagged by in_analysis, and exclusion_reason gives the reason for each of the 13 excluded). Includes symptom classification, urinalysis, culture, sequencing depth, urotype, seven alpha diversity indices, and SRA run and BioSample accessions. - S3_File_bray_curtis.csv — one row per computed pair of samples (n = 136), in long format. A pair that could not be computed has no row, so no missing-value code is used. - S4_File_data_dictionary.csv — definition of every variable in the three data files. Raw sequence data are deposited separately in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject PRJNA1499220. S2_File_samples.csv maps each sample to its SRA run and BioSample accession. Age, years since diagnosis, etiology and level of injury are reported in aggregate in Table 2 of the paper and are not included here: they are not used in any analysis, and released individually they would uniquely identify most participants in this small single-site cohort. Individual-level demographic data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

title: Isodynamicity as a Dirac Constraint on the Ideal-MHD Lie-Poisson Bracket: a Jalon Addendum on the (Non-) Degeneracy of the Constraint Matrix, from the Axisymmetric X-Point to the Homoclinic Tangle (v2)
abstract: Motivated by correspondence with A. Gruber and Sina (Sandia National Laboratories) on extending Lie-Poisson bracket reductions to semidirect-product groups, and with D. Peralta-Salas (ICMAT) on the geometry of isodynamic equilibria, this Jalon note examines whether the isodynamic constraint ||B||^2 = B_0(\psi)^2 on a magnetic flux surface can be treated as a genuine second-class constraint, à la Dirac, on the noncanonical (Morrison-Greene-Newcomb) Poisson bracket of ideal MHD.Version 2 (September 10, 2026, superseding September 8, 2026 v1) includes:- Formal generalization and symbolic re-verification of the Dirac secondary constraint \Phi_2 and its principal symbol \sigma_{12}(x,k) = -(4|B|^2/\rho)|B x k|^2 across orthogonal curvilinear coordinates (fixing two index/tensor contraction script bugs in the verification pipeline without changing the underlying physical tensor identity).- Corrected numerical validation on a VMEC++ equilibrium of Wendelstein 7-X (fixing a Fourier Nyquist mode indexing error and clarifying the distinction between a local magnetic-well minimum and an island-chain topological X-point).- Negative finding on natural resonance overlap: natural driving harmonics for low-order rational surfaces on W7-X and a ConStellaration quasi-isodynamic equilibrium carry negligible amplitude (~0.03%), placing Chirikov overlap parameters ~30x below the chaos threshold.- A novel hybrid real-field / prescribed-chaos triangulation demonstrating that when a controlled perturbation is applied to realistic 3D metric-weighted fields, all dynamically active directions (resonant wavevector, Lyapunov stretching, unstable homoclinic manifold) remain within 10 degrees of k \perp B, confirming the maximal non-degeneracy of the constraint matrix away from the gauge direction k || B.AI-contribution disclosure: Produced in collaborative dialogue with an AI language model (Anthropic Claude), which assisted with symbolic verification (sympy), numerical integrations, manifold tracing, and VMEC++ equilibrium analysis. All physical framing, decision to pursue and correct conjectures, and responsibility for final content rest with the human author.

title: Analysis of Inner Planet Orbital Azimuth Drift
abstract: The residual perihelion precession of Mercury of 43 arcseconds per century has long been regarded as core observational evidence for spacetime curvature in general relativity. By reviewing historical planetary perturbation calculations and numerical simulation workflows, this residual difference is not an inherent defect within the framework of Newtonian mechanics. Analytical theories by Le Verrier and Newcomb adopted mathematical treatment of full orbital period time averaging, which smoothed out transient strong torques arising from close planetary encounters. Early N body numerical simulations from the 1980s used a fixed 5 day time step, leading to insufficient sampling of short duration strong gravitational pulses and producing implicit numerical averaging effects. Modern DE series ephemerides embed post Newtonian relativistic corrections directly and fit parameters against observational data, creating circular reasoning and making it impossible to obtain genuine perturbation results under a pure Newtonian framework. From the perspective of geometric physics, real perihelion precession corresponds to azimuthal rotation of the empty focus of the ellipse, causing overall displacement of the entire elliptical orbit. Pure orbital deformation only changes orbital eccentricity and produces radial shifts of the empty focus without azimuthal rotation. Mercury possesses the largest orbital eccentricity among the eight planets, and its mass is far smaller than the masses of the Sun, Venus and Earth. Its orbit is highly susceptible to gravitational perturbations from external bodies. The empty focus lies far from the Sun and is extremely sensitive to lateral torques. Actual precession effects concentrate within short time windows during a limited number of close planetary encounters across a century. Whether analytical outputs from period averaging match real physical evolution cannot be determined solely by mathematical derivation. The true physical criterion must come from pure Newtonian long duration N body integration without relativistic corrections and with adaptively refined time steps during near encounter intervals, to identify the real physical origin of the 43 arcsecond residual.

title: Analysis of Inner Planet Orbital Azimuth Drift
abstract: The residual perihelion precession of Mercury of 43 arcseconds per century has long been regarded as core observational evidence for spacetime curvature in general relativity. By reviewing historical planetary perturbation calculations and numerical simulation workflows, this residual difference is not an inherent defect within the framework of Newtonian mechanics. Analytical theories by Le Verrier and Newcomb adopted mathematical treatment of full orbital period time averaging, which smoothed out transient strong torques arising from close planetary encounters. Early N body numerical simulations from the 1980s used a fixed 5 day time step, leading to insufficient sampling of short duration strong gravitational pulses and producing implicit numerical averaging effects. Modern DE series ephemerides embed post Newtonian relativistic corrections directly and fit parameters against observational data, creating circular reasoning and making it impossible to obtain genuine perturbation results under a pure Newtonian framework. From the perspective of geometric physics, real perihelion precession corresponds to azimuthal rotation of the empty focus of the ellipse, causing overall displacement of the entire elliptical orbit. Pure orbital deformation only changes orbital eccentricity and produces radial shifts of the empty focus without azimuthal rotation. Mercury possesses the largest orbital eccentricity among the eight planets, and its mass is far smaller than the masses of the Sun, Venus and Earth. Its orbit is highly susceptible to gravitational perturbations from external bodies. The empty focus lies far from the Sun and is extremely sensitive to lateral torques. Actual precession effects concentrate within short time windows during a limited number of close planetary encounters across a century. Whether analytical outputs from period averaging match real physical evolution cannot be determined solely by mathematical derivation. The true physical criterion must come from pure Newtonian long duration N body integration without relativistic corrections and with adaptively refined time steps during near encounter intervals, to identify the real physical origin of the 43 arcsecond residual.

title: Isodynamicity as a Dirac Constraint on the Ideal-MHD Lie–Poisson Bracket: From the Axisymmetric X-Point to the Homoclinic Tangle
abstract: AbstractMotivated by correspondence with A. Gruber and Sina (Sandia National Laboratories) on ex-tending Lie–Poisson bracket reductions to semidirect-product groups, and with D. Peralta-Salas(ICMAT) on the geometry of isodynamic equilibria, this Jalon note examines whether the isody-namic constraint |B|2 = B0 (ψ)2 on a magnetic flux surface can be treated as a genuine second-class constraint, à la Dirac, on the noncanonical (Morrison–Greene–Newcomb) Poisson bracketof ideal MHD, rather than as a soft penalty term in a stellarator-optimization cost functional.Building on the precedent of Chandre, Morrison & Tassi (2012) for the incompressibility con-straint, we derive the secondary constraint Φ2 = {Φ1 , H} explicitly, verify the underlying vectoridentity symbolically, and compute the leading (principal-symbol) structure of the Dirac matrixC12 (x, y) = {Φ1 (x), Φ2 (y)}. We show that C12 is generically elliptic away from the gauge-typedegeneracy k ∥ B (field-line relabeling), and that — contrary to a heuristic conjecture advancedby the author in preliminary correspondence — the axisymmetric magnetic X-point is not alocus of enhanced degeneracy: it is, in this reduced two-dimensional setting, the point of max-imal ellipticity, since the toroidal field there is exactly orthogonal to every admissible poloidalwavevector. We further test, in a Chirikov two-resonance island-overlap toy model, whetherany dynamically relevant direction — the resonant wavevector, the generic chaotic (Lyapunov)stretching direction, or the actual unstable manifold of the homoclinic tangle — comes closeto the Dirac degeneracy direction k ∥ B. All three land within 10◦ of k ⊥ B, the diametricalopposite, reflecting a structural anisotropy of magnetized plasma dynamics rather than a searchfailure. We present this as a corrected, well-triangulated pessimistic Jalon result, and outlinewhat a genuinely three-dimensional (non-axisymmetric-equilibrium) extension would need toshow to overturn it.AI-contribution disclosure. This note was produced in collaborative dialogue with an AIlanguage model (Anthropic Claude), which assisted with literature retrieval, symbolic verification(via sympy) of the vector identities and tensor contractions in Sec. 3, the numerical toy-modelintegration, Newton-method fixed-point search, and manifold tracing in Sec. 5, and drafting. Allphysical framing, the decision to pursue and then correct the X-point conjecture, the choice toescalate to the two-resonance triangulation, and responsibility for the final content rest with thehuman author. No institutional funding or affiliation supports this work.

title: The Leading Digit Is 1 Three Times in Ten, but Only for Data Spread Across Many Orders of Magnitude ── Among 2^n for n=1 to 10000 the leading digit is 1 in 0.301000 of cases, within 0.000092 of log_10(1+1/d) for all nine digits ── the dividing line is whether the data spread across orders of magnitude ── [Paper 612]
abstract: Counting which of 1 to 9 is the leading digit (the top digit) in a list of numbers often gives about three in ten for 1 and under five per cent for 9 (Benford's law). For which data it holds, and for which it does not, is counted. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──that leading digits are uneven (Newcomb, 1881; Benford, 1938), that the only distribution unchanged by rescaling is this law (Pinkham, 1961), that numbers drawn from a mixture of distributions approach it (Hill, 1995), and that the fractional parts of nlog_102 spread evenly (Weyl, 1916) are all known. Applications are not treated──detecting fraud in accounts and the like are not entered. Why so much real data follows it is not discussed──data that follow and data that do not are only sorted and counted by how far they spread in orders of magnitude. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 117 separated four ways in which scale invariance fixes an exponent──this paper confirms in numbers that, for leading digits, a distribution unchanged by rescaling is log_10(1+1/d). What is added is counting the leading digits of 10000 powers of 2 exactly as integers, setting side by side that tripling changes nothing while doubling uniform numbers changes the shares, and placing the separator on whether the data spread across orders of magnitude, measuring the spread of uniform numbers, heights and products in orders. First, powers of 2 follow Benford's law closely──computing 2^n exactly as integers for n=1 to 10000 and counting leading digits, 1 appears 3010 times (0.301000) and 9 appears 458 times, within 0.000092 of log_10(1+1/d) for all nine digits. The first 5000 Fibonacci numbers also stay within 0.000347 (Section 2). Second, multiplying everything by the same number leaves the distribution unchanged──multiplying all 2^n by 3, the share with leading digit 1 is still 0.301000, with a largest difference of 0.000108 (Section 3). Third, data that do not span orders of magnitude do not follow it──uniform numbers from 1 to below 10 give 0.110675 for leading digit 1 (close to 1/9), and doubling them changes it to 0.554595. Heights averaging 170 cm give almost all (0.999985) leading digit 1 (Section 4). Fourth, and this is the core. The separator is whether the data spread across orders of magnitude──products of 20 uniform numbers from 0 to 1 spread over more than 17 orders of magnitude and give 0.300080 for leading digit 1. Data spread evenly on the scale of digits (the logarithm) keep their distribution under any multiplication and follow log_10(1+1/d); uniform numbers within one order, or heights spread over only 0.170 of an order, do not (Section 4). Counting leading digits in a list of numbers often gives about three in ten for 1. That holds only for data spread across many orders of magnitude──counting 10000 powers of 2 exactly, all nine leading digits were within 0.000092 of log_10(1+1/d), and tripling everything changed nothing, because the fractional parts of nlog_102 spread evenly. The separator is whether the data spread across orders of magnitude──uniform numbers from 1 to 10 are close to 1/9, change to 10/18 when doubled, and heights are almost all 1. Products of 20 uniform numbers spread over more than 17 orders and give 0.300080 for leading digit 1. Placed among the earlier papers──the scale invariance of Paper 117 fixes the shares uniquely for leading digits. To be honest──neither applications nor the theory of why real data follow the law are entered; only counts and comparisons of spread. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. Keywords: Benford's law, leading digit, scale invariance, logarithmic uniformity, spread over orders of magnitude. ----- 数の一覧で、先頭の数字(いちばん上の桁)が 1 から 9 のどれになるかを数えると、1 が約三割、9 が五パーセント足らずになることが多い(ベンフォードの法則)。それがどんなデータで成り立ち、どんなデータで成り立たないかを数える。新しい定理も法則も主張しない。 本稿の射程(射程注記):新しい定理も法則も主張しない──先頭の数字が偏ること(ニューカム、1881/ベンフォード、1938)、何倍しても変わらない分布がこの法則に限られること(ピンカム、1961)、いろいろな分布から取り混ぜた数がこの法則に近づくこと(ヒル、1995)、nlog_102 の小数部分が一様に散ること(ワイル、1916)は、いずれも既知である。応用を扱わない──帳簿の不正の検出などには立ち入らない。なぜ多くの実データが従うかは論じない──従うデータと従わないデータを、桁の広がりで分けて数えるだけである。既刊との関係:論文117 は、スケール不変性が指数を四通りに選ぶことを分けた──本稿は、尺度を変えても変わらない分布が先頭の数字では log_10(1+1/d) になることを、数で確かめる。加えたのは、2^n の先頭の数字を正確な整数で 10000 個数えたこと、3 倍しても変わらないこと、一様な数では 2 倍で変わることを並べたこと、分離子を「桁をまたいで広がるか」に置き、一様・身長・積の広がりを桁で測ったことである。 第一に、2 の冪は、ベンフォードの法則にぴったり従う──2^n を n=1 から 10000 まで正確な整数で計算して先頭の数字を数えると、1 が 3010 回(0.301000)、9 が 458 回で、log_10(1+1/d) との差は九つの数字すべてで 0.000092 以内だった。フィボナッチ数(初めの 5000 個)でも差は 0.000347 以内だった(第2節)。 第二に、全部を同じ数倍しても、分布は変わらない──2^n をすべて 3 倍すると、先頭が 1 の割合はやはり 0.301000 で、差の最大は 0.000108 だった(第3節)。 第三に、桁をまたがないデータは従わない──1 以上 10 未満の一様な数では先頭が 1 の割合は 0.110675(1/9 に近い)で、それを 2 倍すると 0.554595 に変わる。平均 170 cm の身長ではほぼ全部(0.999985)が 1 である(第4節)。 第四に、これが本稿の芯である。分離子は、データが桁をまたいで広がるかどうかである──0 から 1 の一様な数を 20 個掛けた積は 17 桁あまりに広がり、先頭が 1 の割合は 0.300080 だった。桁の目盛り(対数)で見て一様に広がるデータは、何倍しても分布が変わらず、log_10(1+1/d) に従う。1 桁に収まる一様な数や、0.170 桁しか広がらない身長は従わない(第4節)。 数の一覧で先頭の数字を数えると、1 が約三割になることが多い。それは、桁をまたいで広がるデータだけである──2^n を 10000 個正確な整数で数えると、先頭の数字は九つとも log_10(1+1/d) から 0.000092 以内で、全部を 3 倍しても変わらなかった。 nlog_102 の小数部分が一様に散るからである。分離子は、データが桁をまたいで広がるかどうかである──1 から 10 の一様な数は 1/9 に近く、2 倍すると 10/18 に変わり、身長はほぼ全部が 1 だった。20 個の一様な数の積は 17 桁あまりに広がり、先頭が 1 の割合は 0.300080 だった。既刊との位置──論文117 のスケール不変性は、先頭の数字では割合を一つに決める。正直に言えば──応用にも、なぜ実データが従うかの理論にも立ち入っておらず、数え上げと広がりの比較だけである。 作成にあたって:本稿の着想と内容は、著者自身の考察に基づくものです。文章の構成整理や英訳、数式の確認には AI(大規模言語モデル)の助力を得ました。最終的な内容の解釈や誤りがあれば、それらはすべて著者の責に帰します。お気づきの点があれば、ご教示いただければ幸いです。 キーワード:ベンフォードの法則、先頭の数字、尺度不変性、対数の一様分布、桁の広がり。
