title: Fate in Ancient Greek Philosophy and Religion
abstract: The Greek term heimarmene, rendered in Latin as fatum and in English as “fate” (and occasionally as “destiny”), designates a doctrinal notion situated at the intersection of Greek religion and philosophy. The analysis of the interplay between the purported causality of fate and that of other forms of causation is a complex undertaking, closely connected with a range of religious questions. Reflection on fate gives rise to fundamental philosophical issues, including those concerning contingent futures, freedom of the will, determinism, divine foreknowledge, and providence. Furthermore, this theme is intertwined with numerous human situations prominently depicted in Greek epic and tragic literature—indeed, it has exercised a lasting influence on Western literature as a whole. Such situations include unexpected good fortune, the mortal inability to withstand misfortune, the practice of divination, and the relationship between human beings and the divine. Given the enduring relevance of themes such as free will, determinism, and divine foreknowledge within contemporary philosophy of religion, it is particularly fruitful to investigate how these questions were addressed not only by Greek philosophers but also by other Greek authors who are not typically classified as philosophers. In late antiquity, Greek thought revisited the problem of fate and divine providence within the framework of Christian theology, engaging in close dialogue with so-called “pagan” philosophical traditions. These exchanges constitute a significant contribution to the metaphysical understanding of fate.

title: THE NATURE OF TIME: Trialogue of Science Philosophy and Religion Vision of Time
abstract: The phenomenon of time remains one of the most foundational, recalcitrant, and under-determined categories of human inquiry. While the natural sciences successfully formalize and measure the operational properties of time, they lack a universally accepted ontological definition of what time is at the bedrock of Being. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. Part I (Science) identifies the precise junctures at which modern theoretical physics — particularly the problem of time in quantum gravity, the cosmological singularity, and the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems — reaches the outer boundary of empirical formalisms.Part II (Philosophy) constructs an autonomous metaphysical architecture upon this threshold: a three-tiered taxonomy of temporality (causal TIME-1, cyclical Time-2, and evental/phenomenal time-3). From this foundation the work develops a periodic scale of temporal densities, an ontology of organic lifespan governed by discrete chronon allocations, a ninefold intentional matrix of temporal perception, and an account of civilizational and spiritual impetus.Part III (Religion) establishes a sustained conceptual dialogue with the Abrahamic traditions and formulates the structural paradigm of the “ascending spiral” as a rigorous alternative to the exhausted dichotomy between linear-historical and cyclical-cosmological temporalities. The original contribution of the dissertation does not consist in a claim to resolve open technical problems of theoretical physics — a pretension the work explicitly rejects. Its novelty resides in the overarching architecture of the synthesis: the three-tiered taxonomy as an epistemological instrument capable of sustaining physics, phenomenology, and theology in coherent relation without domain conflation, and the model of the ascending spiral as a conceptual bridge reconciling eternity, cosmic periodicity, and teleological becoming. The final chapters integrate this architecture within the author’s paradigm of Informational Monism.

title: Axiality and Pluralism: Karl Jaspers and the Search for a Global Philosophy of Religion
abstract: Abstract The paper addresses the concepts of globality, universality, and pluralism in contemporary philosophy of religion. We argue that embracing a form of pluralism is essential to meet the growing demand for inclusivity in the philosophical study of religions, although this does not equate with any rejection of the classic Western tradition. To support this argument, we explore Karl Jaspers’ notion of the Axial Age ( Achsenzeit ) and its relevance to this discussion. We begin with a brief overview of the theory, emphasizing the religious elements it encompasses and its implications. The Axial Age is recognized as a period during which both major world religions and diverse spiritual experiences and practices emerged. This significance becomes particularly evident in contemporary discussions by authors such as Jan Assmann and Jürgen Habermas. We therefore propose that the Axial Age could serve as a useful model for the philosophy of religion. However, we also note that it requires substantial modifications. On one hand, the concept is more Eurocentric than it initially appears; on the other hand, it is inherently open to a truly global perspective and can effectively describe various forms of religiosity. As proof of this thesis, we conclude by focusing on the connection between these issues and the themes of secularization and post-secularization.

title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative. It concludes that mercy, as enacted in John 8:1-11, does not violate justice but fulfills it by restoring moral order in a manner that preserves both human dignity and ethical responsibility.

title: The Origins of R. G. Collingwood's Philosophy of History in his Philosophy of Religion, 1916–1943
abstract: Abstract This article argues that R.G. Collingwood's philosophy of history was deeply rooted in his early philosophy of religion as expounded in Religion and Philosophy (1916). Although scholars have tended to separate Collingwood's early religious ideas from his later writings, this study demonstrates that his theory of history was informed by his endeavour to solve the theological problems raised by what he regarded as the reductionism of two Oxford philosophical schools: realism and idealism. In response, he defended a conception of thought as a qualitatively distinct, irreducible activity, enabling him to reinterpret central Christian doctrines, such as the incarnation and atonement, in historical terms. Christ's omniscience, for example, was reconceived as the knowledge of a perfect historian who understood human motives without predetermining them. This dualist conception of thought prefigured the metaphysical premise of his later theory that history was the re‐enactment of past thoughts. The article traces how these themes, first articulated in theological contexts, informed his later works from Speculum Mentis (1924) to the Essay on Metaphysics (1940). It concludes that the origins of Collingwood's philosophy of history cannot be separated from his philosophy of religion: both emerged from a defence of human freedom, historical meaning, and Christian theism.

title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

title: Religion and alienation: towards posing of the probleme
abstract: In the philosophy of religion, the theme of alienation is used rather narrowly, mainly in connection with its sociocentric interpretations, as well as in the context of German classical idealism and materialism. In fact, it turns out that the phenomena behind alienation theories are fundamental and quite universal in the history of human thought. One shall not be wondered by the case that philosophy tends to deal with just such things. The article examines concepts of alienation in the religion studies, and issues related to them in the works of Plotinus, Kant, Hegel, Schelling, Feuerbach, Marx, Kierkegaard, Nesmelov, Nietzsche, and Girard. It is demonstrated that the diversity of approaches to the problem is due to the difference in axiomatic assumptions or to what is taken as basic experience. As a review of concepts, the article aims to show the possibilities of a "cartographic" approach in teaching philosophy of religion.

title: Relational Emergence Theory： A Hierarchical Emergent Cosmological Model Based on Relational Ontology
abstract: This paper proposes "Relational Emergence Theory," which asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but "relation." Relations continuously derive across different scales, and the process of derivation itself constitutes spacetime. Humans, along with their perception, logic, science, philosophy, and religion, are all localized self-observational phenomena within this relational network. This paper demonstrates the compatibility of this framework with physics, mathematics, biology, cognitive science, philosophy, and religion, and responds to challenges from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, quantum entanglement, Yogācāra Buddhism, the God hypothesis, and nihilism. The paper concludes that although this framework does not provide new observable predictions, it offers a meta-theory capable of delineating boundaries for existing disciplines and indicating ways in which they interconnect, while simultaneously providing a naturalistic foundation for questions of human meaning.

title: Worship-Worthiness First
abstract: Abstract This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion. To develop this claim, I divide the philosophy of worship into two branches: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God). After developing a tripartite account of worship, I distinguish two broad theological approaches: Worship-Worthiness Theology (WWT), which takes worship-worthiness as its organizing concern, and Non-Worship-Worthiness Theology (NWWT), which begins from other metaphysical or theological priorities. I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First. I argue that this thesis can transform existing debates in the philosophy of religion. I develop this thesis through three case studies: perfect being theism, arguments for God’s existence, and the nature of God. Worship-worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

title: Religious non-realism: expanding an idea
abstract: Abstract In this study, I seek to rehabilitate the notion of ‘religious non-realism’, which is misunderstood in the philosophy of religion and significantly underdeveloped. I begin by widening the scope of the idea to encompass both propositional and non-propositional phenomena, and then focus on non-realist religious practice, expanding beyond what I call discourse-centred practices – focused on mobilizing substitutes for realist interpretations of religious discourse; expressivism and fictionalism suggest examples – to practices whose non-realism is discourse-independent. Once discourse-independent non-realist practices are acknowledged, a further distinction presents itself. Non-realist religious practice may be governed by a single idea – such as an expressivist or fictionalist idea – or it may integrate multiple such ideas. I call the former sort of non-realism monist and the latter mixed . Taken together, these distinctions reveal a range of structurally distinct forms of non-realist (and thus non-believing) religion, including mixed possibilities that have received no attention in the literature. By bringing the latter into view through concrete examples drawn primarily from Christianity, the study shows that the discussion of non-realist religious practice admits of a richer depiction, and one perhaps also more true to life, than philosophy of religion has so far supplied.

title: Miracle Money and Contemporary Nigerian Pentecostalism: A Philosophical Analysis of Matthew 17:24-27
abstract: The contemporary doctrine of miracle money has become a notable feature of some Nigerian Pentecostalism, with Matthew 17:24-27 frequently invoked to justify expectations of supernatural financial provision. Despite its growing influence, the doctrine has received limited philosophical scrutiny, particularly regarding its epistemological justification and hermeneutical legitimacy. This study examines the relationship between the Matthean narrative of the coin in the fish's mouth and the contemporary doctrine of miracle money from the perspective of the philosophy of religion. Employing a qualitative methodology that integrates philosophical analysis with contextual biblical hermeneutics, the study critically evaluates the epistemic basis of miracle claims, the interpretive movement from biblical narrative to doctrine, and the ethical implications of contemporary Pentecostal teaching. The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision. It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant. The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief. The paper contributes to ongoing debates in the philosophy of religion by clarifying the relationship between biblical interpretation, miracle claims, and contemporary Pentecostal doctrine.
venue: IRASS Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences

title: Género: una mirada desde la filosofía griega y las religiones
abstract: Feminist and gender theories have shown that gender, as a cultural construct, influences daily, social, and political life. Philosophy has debated knowledge, ethics, and values, and has assigned different ontological value to men and women, while religions, throughout history, have established patriarchy as a social system, with men as heads of households and owners of property. It was not until the 20th century, with the formalization of feminist and gender studies, that the fundamentalist conceptions of philosophy and religion were refuted and various theories were developed to explain gender differences from a scientific perspective, drawing on various social and natural sciences.
venue: Inventio, la génesis de la cultura universitaria en Morelos

title: Druidry and Priority Polytheism
abstract: Abstract This paper will focus on conceptions of the divine in Modern Druidry. While acknowledging the diversity among Druids in their beliefs about the divine, this paper will have a particular focus on forms of polytheism that include belief in some form of ultimate divinity in addition to the pantheon of gods and goddesses. I will propose a way of understanding how such views can work through engagement with the priority monist view in metaphysics, using this view to construct a version of polytheism called priority polytheism. Following this, I will anticipate and respond to some objections to priority polytheism. Through this, this paper will show how engagement with Druidry in contemporary philosophy of religion can yield fruitful results.

title: Academic Portfolio: International Invitations, Peer-Reviewed Acceptances & Editorial Service (2025–2026)
abstract: Introduction This portfolio documents my academic activities during 2025–2026 as an independent researcher from Algeria. All conferences and events listed here are non-profit university events, and all presented papers underwent peer review prior to acceptance. All these research contributions and participations are grounded in a single unified theoretical framework: the equation F + B = Nf (the B-Bouzid model and the concept of Internal Sovereignty F), which has been applied across multiple academic disciplines covered by these conferences, including neurophilosophy, liberal education, artificial intelligence, ethics, and philosophy of religion. title: জঞনতততব ও ধরমতততবর আলক সতয : একট তলনমলক আলচন (The Concept of Truth in Epistemology and Theology: A Comparative Discussion)
abstract: The concept of truth is one of the central themes in both philosophy and theology. Epistemology and theology have advanced in the pursuit of truth with different methods and distinct objectives. Consequently, their presentations of truth also different. This paper attempts to analyze the nature and purpose of truth in the light of epistemology and theology. It discusses the methods and sources employed by philosophy and religion in justifying truth. On this discussion, the paper identifies possible areas of conflict between the two conceptions and proposes constructive solutions for resolving them. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate, through comparative analysis, that although epistemological and theological truths are distinct, they can complement each other and can play a vital role in flourishing human life.

title: Prospettive di Storia di Filosofia della Religione. Per un confronto critico tra Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani
abstract: Il saggio propone un confronto critico tra le prospettive filosofiche di Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani, con particolare rilievo per l’interpretazione che i due autori delineano del Concilio Vaticano II. Il testo si articola in tre sezioni: nella prima imposto in breve la metodologia utilizzata, sottolineando l’opportunità di un’analisi storico-culturale anche per la filosofia della religione; nella seconda istituisco un serrato raffronto tra Caracciolo e Piovani, specie per quanto attiene la pubblicazione de La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) e la sua discussione da parte del filosofo napoletano (poi raccolta nel volume dell’anno successivo Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); l’ultima sezione è invece interamente dedicata all’interpretazione conciliare. Parole chiave: Filosofia della religione, Filosofia della storia, Alberto Caracciolo, Pietro Piovani, Concilio Vaticano II The essay proposes a critical comparison between Alberto Caracciolo and Pietro Piovani, with a particular emphasis on the interpretation that the two authors outline of the Second Vatican Council. The text is divided into three sections: in the first, I briefly set out the methodology used, emphasizing the appropriateness of a historical-cultural analysis of the philosophy of religion; in the second I establish a close comparison between Caracciolo and Piovani, especially concerning the publication of La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) and its discussion by the Neapolitan philosopher (later collected in Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); the last section is instead entirely devoted to the Council’s interpretation. Keywords: Philosophy of Religion, Philosophy of History, Alberto Caracciolo, Pietro Piovani, Second Vatican Council
venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)

title: JCRT Book Review Section Relaunched
abstract: The editorial board of the Journal for Cultural and Religious Theory (JCRT), a Whitestone Publication, is pleased to announce the relaunch of its book review program. Effective immediately, JCRT is soliciting single-title reviews and cluster reviews from scholars working across religious studies, theology, philosophy of religion, critical theory, and adjacent fields. The relaunch responds directly to the void left by the closure of Reading Religion, the American Academy of Religion's openly accessible book review site, which ceased active operations on May 31, 2026. With one of the largest open venues for scholarly religion reviews now transitioned to an archive, JCRT aims to help fill that gap by offering an open-access, peer-edited home for rigorous, timely, and theoretically engaged reviews.

title: Semantic Appraisal of Blessing and the Sacred in Contemporary Philosophy of Language and Religion
abstract: This paper examines the semantic status of blessing and the sacred from the perspectives of contemporary philosophy of language and philosophy of religion. It considers four approaches to these concepts and distinguishes between theories that understand meaning primarily through reference and those that understand meaning through relations within broader linguistic and conceptual networks. Drawing on debates concerning referentialism, semantic holism, contextualism, and religious language, the analysis asks whether blessing and the sacred can be understood without assuming independently existing referents. It also considers the role of belief attribution and the wider importance of semantics for the study of religion. The paper argues that non-referential and holistic approaches provide useful resources for interpreting religious concepts while allowing questions concerning their ontological referents to remain open.
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: After Clarity Comes Return: A Pilot Method for Mapping Tawbah, Inabah, Moral Repair, and Accountability in Qur'anic Discourse
abstract: This paper develops and tests a pilot method for mapping the burden of clarity in Qur'anic argument. The study begins from a methodological problem in Qur'anic studies and philosophy of religion: the Qur'an repeatedly presents guidance as clarification, proof, sign, reminder, and argument, yet discussions of proof often move too quickly from isolated verses to apologetic conclusion, doctrinal assertion, or devotional reflection. What remains underdeveloped is a disciplined way to ask how clarity becomes morally binding inside the discourse itself. When does a text portray a listener as merely uninformed, and when does it portray that listener as already addressed, shown, warned, reminded, and therefore answerable? The paper proposes a structured coding model for bayyinah, hujjah, burhan, ayah, bayan, and related evidential terms as they function in Qur'anic argument. The model does not treat these terms as interchangeable synonyms. It distinguishes manifest clarity, demonstrative proof, binding argument, sign-based indication, explanatory disclosure, warning, response demand, and excuse closure. The pilot method records the type of clarity being presented, the addressee being addressed, the resistance being exposed, the response demanded, the threshold of accountability, and the evidential strength of the claim. Selected passage clusters are used to test whether this method can map the Qur'an's movement from communication to responsibility without reducing revelation to a mechanical argument chart or turning moral accountability into an unsupported judgment about actual persons. The findings suggest that Qur'anic argument often treats clarity not as bare information but as an event of moral exposure. A sign may invite reflection, a reminder may reactivate knowledge, a proof may answer objection, a messenger may remove the claim of ignorance, and a clear evidence may transform neutrality into responsibility. The contribution of the paper is methodological and philosophical: it offers a replicable way to study how Qur'anic discourse forms answerability through clarity while preserving interpretive caution. The model is designed to support Qur'anic studies, hermeneutics, philosophy of religion, and moral epistemology by separating textual observation from theological judgment, evidential claim from rhetorical force, and public method from private verdict.

title: Genealogies of Race and Religion in Kant
abstract: Immanuel Kant is synonymous with modernity, enlightenment and secularity. This reputation is earned through the incredible influence of his three weighty critiques, which have laid the intellectual, moral and aesthetic foundations for modern philosophical thought. Despite this reputation, many scholars in recent years have argued that Kant’s intellectual contribution to secularism, moral universality and political republicanism ought to be approached more critically. The ‘other’ Kant is also one of the progenitors of the modern concept of race. Kantians have defended Kant against charges that race is essential to his entire critical project. This essay moves beyond the stalemate between race scholars and Kantians by reading his concept of race together with his philosophy of religion. Drawing on critical approaches to religion, race and secularism, this essay argues that race is constitutive of his philosophy. More specifically, it demonstrates how race and religion are deeply entangled in Kant’s construction of Jews and Judaism as the constitutive outsiders of Euro-Christian modernity.

title: The Existence of God: A New Way
abstract: Abstract This article addresses the ‘discrepancy issue’ in contemporary analytic philosophy of religion, whereby Richard Swinburne’s probabilistic approach and Graham Oppy’s worldview analysis reach opposing conclusions from substantially the same evidence. In response, it sketches a new abductive argument for God’s existence by developing Peter Lipton’s notion of Inference to the Best Explanation into the method of ‘Virtue-IBE’, which compares rival theories by scoring their theoretical virtues. Virtue-IBE is offered as an improvement upon existing approaches and is applied to Bare Theism, as developed by Swinburne, Worldview Naturalism, as defended by Oppy, and Trope-Theoretic Theism, as proposed in this work (and earlier work), across six broad features of the physical world. On this assessment, Trope-Theoretic Theism, which identifies God as a maximal power trope, emerges as the loveliest, and therefore the best, of the three theories considered. The resulting conjunction of method and theory ultimately provides the basis for a new abductive case for God’s existence.

title: Charles Hodge Defends Sola Gratia: Certainty, Free Will, and God’s Eternal Decree
abstract: This article argues that Charles Hodge’s account of free will offers a neglected alternative to the dominant contemporary binary between determinism and libertarian freedom. Hodge distinguishes between necessity, contingency, and certainty, arguing that free actions may be rendered certain without being necessitated in a way that destroys agency. Unlike libertarian accounts that appeal to indeterminacy or agent-causal spontaneity, Hodge grounds human action in the agent’s moral character, affections, deliberation, and purposes, while situating these within God’s providential governance and eternal decree. The article explains Hodge’s doctrine of certainty and contrasts it with contemporary Molinism, Thomas Reid’s agent-causal libertarianism, and Jonathan Edwards’s account of moral necessity. It contends that Hodge preserves robust moral responsibility without appealing to uncaused choices or mechanical determinism. Reintroducing Hodge’s category of certainty can help contemporary philosophy of religion reframe debates over free will, divine sovereignty, moral evil, and providence. Ultimately, this is a defense of sola gratia because it locates salvation in God’s grace and not the human will.

title: Philosophical Theology: The Basics
abstract: What is philosophical theology? How does philosophy relate to theology? Should theology be philosophical? This book explores answers to these questions from the ancient world to the present day, introducing the reader to the basic theories and thinkers in philosophical theology, within the Judaeo-Christian tradition. The book guides readers through the basic theories and thinkers in western philosophical theology from Plato to Plantinga, presenting key concerns that have led to debates within secular and Christian philosophy throughout history and encouraging readers to engage with these debates. It explores theories and schools of thought that have been developed to try and answer some of the most pressing questions in philosophy and theology across the following areas: faith and knowledge arguments for the existence of God mysticism religious language and experience the soul and life after death good and evil conscience and religious ethics human freewill divine providence and miracles Accessibly written, this book is an ideal starting point for anyone seeking a full introduction to philosophical theology as well as broader themes in philosophy of religion and systematic theology.

title: Paganism in the philosophical reflection of Edward Herbert
abstract: The aim of the research is to identify the significance of Edward Herbert of Cherbury's work "The Religion of the Gentiles" for the development of the philosophy of religion and religious studies. The article examines the source base, methods, and content of Herbert's book, in which the author took the study of religion beyond confessional boundaries. At the core of Herbert's philosophical study lies an attempt to justify paganism by proving the unity of the essential religious foundations of all confessions of the past and present. The scientific novelty of the study is associated with the fact that Herbert's book "The Religion of the Gentiles" is considered for the first time as a methodological attempt to substantiate a universal religion based on cross-cultural comparison. As a result of the study, it was established that the book "The Religion of the Gentiles", firstly, is one of the extensive encyclopedias of religious traditions of its time; secondly, it continues and develops Herbert's teaching on a single universal religious foundation; thirdly, the issues raised in the book define religion as an object of philosophical reflection; fourthly, Herbert bases his conclusions not only on the use of diverse sources, but also on comparative analysis, which brings his study closer to the scientific standards of comparative religious studies.

title: Nothing in God
abstract: Classical monotheism describes God as infinite, all-having, and necessarily existent. This paper asks whether these three descriptions can be held together when “all-having” is read strictly, so that it covers not only everything that is but also non-being. I defend a conditional thesis: if divine infinity requires strict inclusion of non-being itself (and not merely of a representation of it), then strict all-inclusiveness, necessary existence, and classical logic cannot all be true of God. The thesis yields a dilemma for theism: either divine all-inclusiveness must be restricted (for instance, to being and to perfections), or God must be placed beyond the constraints of logic. I offer three routes toward the key premise (a completeness argument, a comparison between two conceptions of God, and an argument from specific privations), examine the main objections, and relate the argument to Tillich’s treatment of non-being in God, Cantor’s Absolute Infinite, dialetheic theology, and Aquinas’s objection from contraries. I do not claim to refute theism. The result is a constraint on how the divine attributes may be defined together. Keywords: divine infinity; non-being; necessary existence; omni-inclusiveness; dialetheism; philosophy of religion

title: Presentazione. Rifrazioni dal pensiero di Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi
abstract: A trent’anni dalla morte di Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi, il contributo intende richiamare alcuni nuclei fondamentali del suo pensiero e introdurre i saggi raccolti nel fascicolo. Dall’ontologismo critico di Pantaleo Carabellese fino alla formulazione del Cristianesimo-Filosofia, il percorso morettiano si sviluppa come ricerca speculativa del fondamento e come esperienza di verità. I contributi approfondiscono, da prospettive differenti, il rapporto con Carabellese, i temi dell’ascesi, della persona, della mondanità, della verità e le connessioni con l’estetica, l’etica, la filosofia della religione e la teologia. Thirty years after the death of Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi, this contribution recalls some of the fundamental themes of his thought and introduces the essays collected in this issue. From Pantaleo Carabellese’s critical ontologism to the formulation of Christianity-Philosophy, Moretti-Costanzi’s philosophical path develops as a speculative inquiry into foundation and as an experience of truth. The contributions examine, from different perspectives, his relationship with Carabellese, as well as the themes of ascesis, personhood, worldliness, truth, and the connections with aesthetics, ethics, philosophy of religion, and theology.
venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)

title: Christian Philosophy and Christian Apologetics: A Philosophical Examination of Their Relationship and Complementarity
abstract: In an increasingly pluralistic and sceptical global context, Christianity continues to face sustained intellectual challenges that question its truth claims, coherence, and relevance. These challenges arise not only from overt secularism but also from competing religious worldviews and internal misunderstandings regarding the role of reason in faith. Within this climate, Christian apologetics emerges as a disciplined response aimed at offering rational justification for Christian belief, while Christian philosophy provides the conceptual and methodological framework through which such justification becomes intelligible. This paper examines the relationship between Christian philosophy and Christian apologetics, arguing that the two disciplines are neither identical nor autonomous, but fundamentally interdependent. Through conceptual analysis, historical reflection, and philosophical engagement, the study demonstrates that apologetics depends on philosophical reasoning for coherence, while Christian philosophy finds practical expression and relevance through apologetic engagement. Drawing on key thinkers in philosophy of religion and Christian thought, the paper contends that a robust defence of Christian faith requires philosophical depth grounded within a Christological and biblical framework. The paper concludes that separating Christian apologetics from Christian philosophy weakens both disciplines and undermines the intellectual credibility of Christian faith in contemporary discourse.
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE

title: Academic Portfolio: International Invitations, Peer-Reviewed Acceptances & Editorial Service (2025–2026)
abstract: This portfolio documents a selection of my academic activities during 2025–2026 as an independent researcher from Algeria. Throughout this journey, I have strictly committed to submitting only to rigorous, non-profit university events, deliberately avoiding predatory or for-profit conferences. My primary objective was never the mere accumulation of acceptances; rather, it was to subject my unified theoretical framework the equation (B)+(F)=Nf (the B-Bouzid model and the concept of Internal Sovereignty F) to rigorous testing across the widest possible diversity of disciplines, audiences, and topics. Crucially, I did not send a single generic abstract to all venues. Instead, I carefully selected each conference and wrote a tailored abstract specifically designed to address the unique epistemological questions and academic language of that specific discipline. Each submission was an experiment: Can a single unified framework genuinely speak to neurophilosophy, quantum physics, liberal education, AI ethics, care ethics, feminist justice, and philosophy of religion alike? For the same reason, rejection was never merely a disappointment; it was data. I frequently inquired about the reasons for rejection to refine my framing, and I was genuinely pleased when a submission faced conditional acceptance or rigorous pushback, as pressure is the ultimate laboratory for any philosophical rule. Important Notes: • Screenshots and official conference links are included in this file. • All official invitation letters and certificates are included in this file as documented proof of these academic participations.

title: An Information-Processing Framework for Substrates of Consciousness: A Naturalistic Approach to Humans, Artificial Intelligence, and the Question of God
abstract: This paper presents an information-processing framework for examining consciousness across biological and artificial substrates. It treats humans and artificial intelligence as information-processing systems implemented on different physical substrates and evaluates claims using methodological naturalism, testability, consistency with established knowledge, and parsimony. The paper examines the epistemic status of several questions at the intersection of philosophy of mind, consciousness science, artificial intelligence, and philosophy of religion. It reviews arguments concerning an interventionist God, including the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, religious diversity, cognitive explanations of religious belief, causal closure, and major theistic responses. It then reviews evidence concerning the dependence of human mental states on brain activity, major scientific theories of consciousness, and current approaches to assessing possible machine consciousness. A further section examines the hypothesis of consciousness transfer between biological and artificial substrates, including questions concerning functionalism, substrate independence, personal identity, whole-brain emulation, and gradual replacement. The paper's main methodological contribution is an epistemic grading framework that distinguishes empirical, theoretical, and philosophical claims according to their evidential support, testability, consistency, and parsimony. The framework emphasizes the distinction between what is empirically established, what is theoretically plausible, and what remains speculative or philosophically contested. This work is a conceptual analysis and literature review rather than an experimental study. It is presented as an open-access research paper and is not represented as a peer-reviewed journal publication.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Kant’s Metaphysical Framework: A Critical Study in the Context of the Islamic Conception of Knowledge and Ethics
abstract: This study presents a critical analysis of Immanuel Kant’s metaphysical framework, with particular reference to his theory of knowledge, conception of reason, philosophy of religion, and moral philosophy. It examines the relationship between Kant’s epistemology and his understanding of religion, particularly his distinction between theoretical and practical reason and his restriction of the scope of human reason in metaphysical matters. The study argues that Kant’s separation of faith and reason is closely connected with the intellectual context of rationalist metaphysics and Christian theology. In contrast, the Islamic intellectual tradition approaches knowledge through an integrated relationship among reason, revelation, and human nature (fiṭrah). The study further examines Kant’s moral philosophy, particularly his conception of pure practical reason, the categorical imperative, duty, freedom, and moral responsibility. It argues that morality cannot be adequately grounded in abstract rational principles alone, since moral consciousness, the distinction between good and evil, and the capacity for moral responsibility are rooted in the human self (nafs) and its innate disposition. Drawing upon Qur’anic teachings and Islamic intellectual thought, the study proposes that revelation does not negate innate human knowledge but completes and reinforces the moral and intellectual awareness embedded in human nature. The study concludes that the Islamic conception of knowledge and ethics provides an integrated framework in which reason, revelation, fiṭrah, and the human self operate in a mutually complementary relationship, offering an alternative perspective to Kant’s restricted conception of reason, morality, and metaphysical knowledge.

title: Methodological Potential of J. Waardenburg's Neo-Phenomenology for Contemporary Religious Studies
abstract: The article examines the methodological potential of Jacques Waardenburg's neo-phenomenology for contemporary philosophy of religion and religious studies. The relevance of the topic is determined by the need to combine empirical rigor in the analysis of religious facts with attention to the meanings that these facts acquire for believers, religious authorities and communities. The purpose of the article is to clarify the extent to which Waardenburg's project can be operationalized without turning it into a closed universal method. To achieve this purpose, the paper analyzes the transition from religion as a system to religion as an interpreted practice, the actor-oriented perspective, and the problems of subjective meaning, intention, context and verification of scholarly interpretation. The methodological basis of the study includes historical analysis of religious studies, conceptual reconstruction, comparative methodology and hermeneutic analysis. The novelty of the article lies in interpreting Waardenburg's neo-phenomenology as a transitional methodology that combines phenomenological attention to meaning with hermeneutic understanding, analysis of actors and the requirement of source-based verification. As a result, the article proposes an operational model that includes identifying a religious fact, describing its context, identifying actors, reconstructing subjective meaning, analyzing intention, comparing the reconstruction with self-descriptions, verifying it through sources, correlating understanding with explanation and explicitly marking interpretive limits. The paper concludes that the value of Waardenburg's project lies not in a finished technique, but in a research framework that helps preserve the balance between the meaning of religious life and scholarly verifiability.

title: From “Li (理)–Mind/Nature (心/性)” to “Qi (气)–History (史)”: The Religious Dimension of Wang Fuzhi’s Qi (气)-Centered Confucianism
abstract: Contemporary debates over whether Confucianism should be regarded as a religion are often constrained by the Western binary opposition between philosophy and religion. Rather than remaining within this classificatory framework, this article shifts attention to the question of how the religious dimension of Confucianism is concretely grounded and sustained. By comparing the “li (理)–mind/nature (心/性)” paradigm of Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism with Wang Fuzhi’s “qi (气)–history (史)” paradigm, the article argues that the former relies primarily on inward moral experience and the self-cultivation of mind and nature, a mode that can effectively uphold a meaningful order under relatively stable historical conditions. By contrast, in response to the rupture of the Ming-Qing transition, Wang Fuzhi relocates ultimate normativity within the dynamic process of qi (气) transformation and historical practice. Through four interrelated formulations—“li (理) resides in qi (气),” “nature (性) is the principle of life,” “principle is to be pursued in concrete affairs,” and “historical reflection as verification”—he provides moral and value judgments with a stronger grounding in lived reality and historical testing. In this way, Wang effects a significant transformation in the religious dimension of Confucianism, shifting it from a mode of inward justification to one of worldly verification. His thought thus offers a more historically resilient account of how Confucian meaning can endure amid times of profound upheaval.

title: Academic Portfolio: International Invitations, Peer-Reviewed Acceptances & Editorial Service (2025–2026)
abstract: This portfolio documents a selection of my academic activities during 2025–2026 as an independent researcher from Algeria. Throughout this journey, I have strictly committed to submitting only to rigorous, non-profit university events, deliberately avoiding predatory or for-profit conferences. My primary objective was never the mere accumulation of acceptances; rather, it was to subject my unified theoretical framework the equation (B)+(F)=Nf (the B-Bouzid model and the concept of Internal Sovereignty F) to rigorous testing across the widest possible diversity of disciplines, audiences, and topics. Crucially, I did not send a single generic abstract to all venues. Instead, I carefully selected each conference and wrote a tailored abstract specifically designed to address the unique epistemological questions and academic language of that specific discipline. Each submission was an experiment: Can a single unified framework genuinely speak to neurophilosophy, quantum physics, liberal education, AI ethics, care ethics, feminist justice, and philosophy of religion alike? For the same reason, rejection was never merely a disappointment; it was data. I frequently inquired about the reasons for rejection to refine my framing, and I was genuinely pleased when a submission faced conditional acceptance or rigorous pushback, as pressure is the ultimate laboratory for any philosophical rule. title: ẸSÌN IS NOT RELIGION: A CONCEPTUAL AND EPISTEMOLOGICAL DISTINCTION IN YORÙBÁ-NIGERIAN THOUGHT
abstract: This paper challenges the routine translation of the Yorùbá word ẹ̀sìn as "religion," an equivalence that has become deeply entrenched in both scholarly and everyday usage. The English term "religion" carries the weight of a specifically Western intellectual lineage shaped by Latin Christendom, post-Reformation denominationalism, and the Enlightenment's rigid separation of sacred and secular spheres. By contrast, ẹ̀sìn arose from a Yorùbá worldview in which cosmology, ethics, ritual practice, and social structure were inseparably intertwined. The study maintains that the modern conflation of ẹ̀sìn with "religion" stems principally from nineteenth-century missionary translation projects and colonial knowledge systems, which imposed foreign assumptions about personal belief, institutional demarcation, and exclusive religious allegiance onto indigenous Yorùbá conceptual frameworks. In methodological terms, the research combines historical-linguistic investigation with close textual analysis of selected Ifá verses to retrieve the indigenous semantic strata of ẹ̀sìn. Theoretically, it draws upon decolonial critique and hermeneutical philosophy of religion. Special emphasis is placed on how ẹ̀sìn appears and functions within the Ifá corpus, examining its significance through its ritual and moral settings rather than through externally imposed doctrinal lenses. By situating the term within its original epistemic milieu, the paper shows that ẹ̀sìn denotes a lived ethical disposition and a structured way of communal existence rather than a circumscribed body of beliefs. Ultimately, the study urges scholars to exercise terminological care and to accord proper respect to indigenous conceptual categories when examining African religious thought.

title: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق — A Human Transformation Framework: Institutional Research & Framework Edition
abstract: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق is a fourteen-stage human transformation framework developed by Syed Raheel Shahzad. It approaches questions of existence, knowledge, belief, human identity, moral responsibility, inner formation, social obligation, and prophetic guidance as parts of a connected system rather than as isolated subjects. The framework begins before inherited labels or doctrinal assumptions, with the question of reality itself: what exists, why anything exists at all, and what follows if reality has an intelligible Source. From that starting point, the system moves through the necessity and authority of revelation, Tawheed and competing forms of allegiance, divine decree and human choice, the meaning of worldly life, identity beyond socially assigned labels, the architecture of the inner self, human formation, rights and responsibilities, and the prophetic trajectories represented by Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ. The publication presents the architecture, sequence, intellectual purpose and human function of all fourteen stages of the Source of Truth System. It also situates the framework within the wider authored library of Syed Raheel Shahzad, including The Architect’s Protocol, The Qur’anic Coherence System, Adam and the Answerable Being, and Tomorrow Became a Country. Rather than treating knowledge as an accumulation of disconnected information, the Source of Truth System asks how truth becomes orientation, how orientation becomes formation, and how formation becomes responsible human action. The framework is intended as an interdisciplinary contribution to systems thinking, philosophy of religion, Islamic thought, epistemology, moral responsibility, identity and human transformation.

title: Beyond Performative Morality Based on A Thematic Interpretation of The Satya-Māyā Dialectic in The Ethics of Power of Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa in The Mahābhārata
abstract: The phenomenon of performative morality and religiosity in the contemporary public sphere (moral and religious expressions intended for public consumption, rather than the manifestation of inner dispositions) highlights the need for a conceptual framework that distinguishes between ethical appearance and substance. This research develops a thematic-hermeneutic reading of the satya-māyā dialectic in the Mahābhārata, examining how Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa represent two opposing ethical orientations within the relationship between truth and power. This study of the philosophy of religion employs a hermeneutic-phenomenological approach to the dice-playing episode in the Sabhā Parva and selected ślokas from the Bhagavad Gītā, combined with a comparative analysis drawing on political realism. The results indicate that Śakuni represents the instrumentalisation of truth and morality as tools of power, whilst Kṛṣṇa articulates an ethic that subordinates power to satya and dharma through niṣkāma karma. Māyā is understood as an epistemological condition that enables the disjunction between appearance and essence, whilst sattva and lokasaṅgraha form the textual basis for leadership with integrity. Performative morality and religiosity are formulated as new analytical categories that bridge performativity theory with the conceptual structure of the Bhagavad Gītā, characterised by the gap between appearance and essence, the instrumentalisation of symbols, and visibility, accompanied by critical scrutiny of Kṛṣṇa’s controversial actions, without theological justification. The research concludes that the Mahābhārata offers a model of the ethics of power that positions truth as the foundation (rather than a tool) of leadership legitimacy; a thesis that holds internally within the text’s cosmology and is relevant by analogy (rather than empirically) to contemporary public ethical reflection.

title: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century
abstract: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century An Agnostic Enlightenment for the Twenty-First Century What remains when inherited certainty begins to fade? For centuries, religious institutions shaped morality, identity, law, and humanity's understanding of existence. Yet the twenty-first century presents an unprecedented reality: scientific progress, democratic institutions, neuroscience, psychology, and universal access to information have profoundly transformed how people approach truth, authority, and belief. In The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century, Northon Salomão de Oliveira offers a bold yet balanced philosophical exploration of this historic transition. Rather than celebrating atheism or defending traditional religion, the book proposes a third path: agnosticism as an intellectual discipline, grounded in evidence, epistemic humility, and the enduring values of the Enlightenment. Drawing inspiration from Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Baron d'Holbach, Karl Popper, Steven Pinker, A. C. Grayling, Martha Nussbaum, Jürgen Habermas, and other influential thinkers, this work examines the decline of religious authority while recognizing the enduring psychological, cultural, and ethical roles that religion has played throughout civilization. Inside, readers will discover: * Why religious dogma is gradually losing its monopoly over truth. * How science, philosophy, and democratic institutions are reshaping moral authority. * The psychological functions religion still fulfills, even in secular societies. * Why agnosticism may represent the most intellectually honest position in an age of uncertainty. * How dogmatic thinking survives beyond religion through ideology, politics, and digital culture. * The unfinished project of building meaning, community, and ethical responsibility without unquestioned authority. Blending philosophy, psychology, history, political theory, cognitive science, and cultural criticism, this book invites readers to confront one of the defining questions of our age: Can humanity preserve meaning, morality, and human dignity after the decline of unquestioned religious authority? Provocative, deeply researched, and written with literary elegance, The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century is an invitation to rethink belief, embrace intellectual honesty, and participate in the continuing Enlightenment of the modern world. This is not a book against faith. It is a book in favor of reason, freedom of inquiry, and the courage to live with honest uncertainty. title: God and Love: Divine Nature in Philosophical, Theological, and Feminist Perspective
abstract: This dissertation draws on philosophical, theological, and feminist resources to offer a novel account of divine love, which renders a transformed view of God, where the divine nature is primarily characterized by love. I begin by arguing for the need of a feminist intervention in contemporary theorizing about the divine nature in Christian analytic philosophy of religion, contending that if we take feminist insights seriously, we ought to carve out a more substantial role for love in the divine nature. Doing so, I argue, requires offering a robust account of divine love and that, to offer such an account, we must first inquire into the nature of love, as such. Regarding love’s nature, I argue for two theses: love is a unified notion with several subtypes (including divine love) and love is primarily a matter of robust care for the beloved, which I further specify in terms of attention, investment, and nurturance. Relating this to the divine nature, I argue that divine love can be understood as a subtype of this account of love, with the stipulation that it involves expression of care fitting to divine perfection. Additionally, I argue for a view of the divine traits on which love plays an enlarged shaping role in the divine nature and show how this view finds solid footing in both Christian scripture and doctrine. Overall, on the proposed account, God is the ideal exemplar of personal love, and divine love is a matter of God’s robust care for creation. To deepen and concretize the account, I address potential objections rooted in concrete experience (i.e., suffering and differences in divine and human love) and draw on scripture to identify expressions, or forms, of divine love and relate these to the account. I conclude by overviewing some key implications of the argument.

title: Self-Awareness, Finitude, and the Structural Necessity of Evil
abstract: This paper presents a framework‑independent modal argument that no possible world can contain self‑aware finite creatures without evil. The result does not rely on any specific theological or metaphysical system. It follows from the structural relationship between three independently defensible claims: (1) genuine finitude entails intrinsic temporal boundedness; (2) self‑awareness entails that one’s own existence is a non‑derivative good; and (3) the privation of a due good is evil. From these premises, the paper demonstrates that wherever self‑aware finite beings exist, death constitutes the necessary privation of a structurally fundamental good — and therefore that evil is not a contingent feature of creaturely worlds but a modal entailment of self‑aware finitude itself. The argument reframes the classical problem of evil. It shows that the standard question — why did God not create self‑aware finite creatures without evil? — presupposes a metaphysically impossible state of affairs. The deeper question becomes what a good ground owes to creatures it necessarily brings into a condition that includes evil. The paper situates its contribution relative to Leibniz, Nagel, Hick, and Smullyan, and identifies self‑awareness as the load‑bearing term missing from earlier accounts. It also clarifies the structural linkage between self‑awareness, finitude, freedom, and death, showing that attempts to remove one term while retaining the others generate incoherent or worse worlds. The argument stands independently of Agápēic Relational Metaphysics (ARM), though ARM provides a deeper explanatory framework for the modal result. The paper is intended for readers in metaphysics, philosophy of religion, modal logic, and any field concerned with the structural conditions of creaturely existence.

title: The Inversion of Greatness
abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being—a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible—this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Rather than assuming modal logic to get the argument off the ground, the book builds that ground first: it derives the claim that whatever is possible is necessarily possible, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility, rather than taking it as a starting axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change requires temporality, spatiality, and physicality, borne by time, space, and substance, and that these three are necessarily instantiated. That structure is what the book calls Nature. From there it argues that no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. The result blocks grounds specified as occupants of that domain, a divine intellect among them, while leaving essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals standing as burdened rather than refuted. The greatness classical theism reserved for God—eternity, self-existence, being the source of all possibility—is relocated to Nature itself, and no determinate, active ground is left able to stand wholly outside Nature while retaining the classical attributes. The argument is then extended outward: to a convergence with contemporary physics in which the cosmological singularity marks a boundary of description rather than a boundary of being; to an account of consciousness as Nature registering itself from within; and to a political theory in which freedom is maximum shared possibility, secured by degree on a floor of material and civic conditions. Along the way the book argues that Reality is nothing over and above Nature. A closing section applies the completed argument to classical theological doctrines, including a new treatment of the problem of evil.

title: Stern, Robert, 1962-2024
abstract: Robert Stern-or Bob, as I cannot resist referring to him in this memoir-was instrumental in shaping British philosophy in the late 20th and early 21st centuries.This was due partly to his unusual interests; or rather, to what were, when he began to nurture them, unusual interests.Many of them became mainstream.Bob himself proffered various explanations for this.Genuine modesty prevented him from acknowledging the significance of his own influence.The interests in question were in the history of philosophy.At the beginning of Bob's career British philosophy was dominated by a species of analytic philosophy that not only proceeded largely independently of the history of the discipline, but involved an element of antipathy towards it.This already made such interests somewhat unusual.But what made them especially so was the cast of philosophers on whom Bob focused, which included (in roughly the order in which he focused on them) G.W.F.Hegel, Søren Kierkegaard, Iris Murdoch, C.S. Peirce, K.E.Løgstrup, and Martin Luther.Some of these, such as Hegel and Kierkegaard, had always been acknowledged as part of the canon, even within the British context in which Bob was working; but they had been considered of purely historical interest and, certainly in Hegel's case, they had been viewed as examples of the absurdities and excesses to which the vagaries of undisciplined philosophical reverie were liable to lead.Others, such as Murdoch and Løgstrup, had not at the time got as far as satisfying even the first of these conditions: that is, they had not yet been acknowledged even as part of the canon.Bob did much to clarify why all of these figures deserved attention-and deserved it for far more than their historical interest.This, combined with their own range, meant that Bob himself made important and historically informed contributions to metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, political philosophy, philosophy of religion, and philosophy of philosophy.He was correspondingly prolific.His publications included: Hegel, Kant and the Structure of the Object; 1 Transcendental Arguments and Scepticism; 2 Understanding Moral Obligation: Kant, Hegel, Kierkegaard; 3 The Routledge Philosophy Guidebook to Hegel and the Phenomenology of Spirit; 4 and The Radical Demand in Løgstrup's Ethics; 5 as well as many other collected volumes, new translations, scholarly editions, and articles.

title: PFUSRC-141 The Complete Topological Ontology of the Dao System and Its Civilizational Positioning — Why Its Era Is Approaching
abstract: Building upon PFUSRC-051 (Mathematical Reduction of the I Ching) and PFUSRC-052 (Textual Authentication of the Daodejing), this paper presents a unified topological ontological framework for Dao, Daoist philosophy, and Daoism as religion, and assesses its contemporary civilizational positioning and future trajectory. Six core conclusions are established: First, within the PFUSRC framework, Dao corresponds to the 45° triple coaxial biconical topological structure at the L4 ontological layer. Daoist philosophy, Daoist religion, and all historical articulations of Dao are multi-layered projections of this structure across different historical periods and social conditions. They are manifestations of a single system, not divisions or degradations. Second, the historical multiplicity of Dao is not confusion but adaptive unfolding under different conditions. The apparent “defects” are necessary costs of projection, which under contemporary conditions are transforming into structural advantages. Third, in horizontal comparison, the Dao system is the only complete system that simultaneously covers all layers from L4 to L7, possesses complete logical closure, and does not depend on external authority. Fourth, the Dao system’s wuwei (non-action) is not inaction but action that does not violate the steady-state path of the 45° biconical topology. Its zhusha (excision) is not violence but topological cleanup—the removal of deviant structures that cannot return to steady-state. First persuade; if persuasion fails, excise—this is the complete operational logic of the Dao system at the projection layer. Fifth, the Dao system’s “reclusive foundation” is not evasion but a survival strategy. By not depending on political structures for its existence, it has never been subject to large-scale suppression. Sixth, in an era when “scar science” (empirical science confined to phenomenological description) is revealing its ontological deficiencies, the Dao system—as the only complete system preserving a dynamic topological cosmology and its practical methodology—is experiencing an irreversible structural ascent. This judgment is not prophecy but structural analysis: when the structure of civilizational needs changes, systems capable of responding to those needs naturally gain attention. The era of the Dao system is approaching, not because it will “defeat” other systems, but because it is already prepared.

title: From Tripartite Freedom to Fair Opportunity: T. H. Green and David O. Brink
abstract: This article examines the structural relationship between T. H. Green’s tripartite conception of freedom and David O. Brink’s fair opportunity account of moral responsibility, arguing that the traces of Green’s model can be discerned in the conceptual architecture of Brink’s account. Green’s conception emerges from a critical engagement with Kant’s account of freedom and responds to Sidgwick’s objection that Kant cannot adequately explain how wrongdoing can be both free and responsible. By identifying moral freedom with the capacity for reasons-responsiveness rather than with its proper exercise, Green defends the spirit of Kantian freedom while addressing its principal weakness. Green distinguishes three dimensions of freedom: juridical freedom as the absence of external coercion; moral freedom as the capacity for reasons-responsiveness that grounds responsibility; and real or perfect freedom as the virtuous actualization of that capacity in pursuit of self-realization and the common good. These three dimensions are not rivals but complementary conditions for the full realization of moral personality. Green’s account of perfect freedom, with its emphasis on self-realization and the common good, also carries a distinctly religious dimension, addressing questions about human nature, divine justice, and moral accountability that situate his tripartite model within the broader concerns of the philosophy of religion. While Berlin’s critique reads Green’s positive freedom as dangerously close to authoritarian justification, and while Weinstein, Simhony, and Dimova-Cookson offer divergent reconstructions of Green’s account, this article takes as its starting point Brink’s reconstruction of Green’s framework within the Kantian tradition. The article shows how Brink’s two central conditions, normative competence and situational control, correspond structurally and substantively to Green’s moral and juridical freedom. It further demonstrates that perfect freedom functions in Brink’s account not as a condition of responsibility but as a post-responsibility ideal of moral excellence that lies beyond the threshold of accountability. Finally, the respect and esteem distinction that Brink develops in dialogue with Kant and Darwall is shown to parallel the difference between moral and perfect freedom. These structural correspondences reflect a philosophically significant continuity between the two thinkers, one that operates not merely at the historical but at the conceptual level.

title: PFUSRC-141 The Complete Topological Ontology of the Dao System and Its Civilizational Positioning — Why Its Era Is Approaching
abstract: Building upon PFUSRC-051 (Mathematical Reduction of the I Ching) and PFUSRC-052 (Textual Authentication of the Daodejing), this paper presents a unified topological ontological framework for Dao, Daoist philosophy, and Daoism as religion, and assesses its contemporary civilizational positioning and future trajectory. Six core conclusions are established: First, within the PFUSRC framework, Dao corresponds to the 45° triple coaxial biconical topological structure at the L4 ontological layer. Daoist philosophy, Daoist religion, and all historical articulations of Dao are multi-layered projections of this structure across different historical periods and social conditions. They are manifestations of a single system, not divisions or degradations. Second, the historical multiplicity of Dao is not confusion but adaptive unfolding under different conditions. The apparent “defects” are necessary costs of projection, which under contemporary conditions are transforming into structural advantages. Third, in horizontal comparison, the Dao system is the only complete system that simultaneously covers all layers from L4 to L7, possesses complete logical closure, and does not depend on external authority. Fourth, the Dao system’s wuwei (non-action) is not inaction but action that does not violate the steady-state path of the 45° biconical topology. Its zhusha (excision) is not violence but topological cleanup—the removal of deviant structures that cannot return to steady-state. First persuade; if persuasion fails, excise—this is the complete operational logic of the Dao system at the projection layer. Fifth, the Dao system’s “reclusive foundation” is not evasion but a survival strategy. By not depending on political structures for its existence, it has never been subject to large-scale suppression. Sixth, in an era when “scar science” (empirical science confined to phenomenological description) is revealing its ontological deficiencies, the Dao system—as the only complete system preserving a dynamic topological cosmology and its practical methodology—is experiencing an irreversible structural ascent. This judgment is not prophecy but structural analysis: when the structure of civilizational needs changes, systems capable of responding to those needs naturally gain attention. The era of the Dao system is approaching, not because it will “defeat” other systems, but because it is already prepared.

title: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? An Epistemological, Historical, and Bayesian Analysis of the Qur'an (2nd ed.).
abstract: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? is a critical study of the Qur’an’s origins through the lens of Bayesian reasoning, historical analysis, and inference to the best explanation. Rather than beginning from either faith or skepticism, the book asks a narrower question: given the evidence available to us, what can actually be established about whether the Qur’an is best explained by genuine divine revelation or by ordinary human and historical processes? The investigation compares competing revelation and human-origin models across a wide range of evidence, including the Qur’an’s Late Antique context, religious geography and diversity, cognition and religious belief, Adam and human evolution, the Flood, alleged textual and legal difficulties, literary inimitability, prophecy, miracle traditions, scientific-miracle claims, textual preservation, Egyptian historical knowledge, and the transmission of hadith. Throughout, the book distinguishes possibility from probability, compatibility from confirmation, undercutting from counterevidence, and local evidential judgments from global conclusions. It also examines how source uncertainty, dependence between arguments, retrospective selection, model flexibility, and differing theological commitments affect the strength of common apologetic and skeptical arguments. The result is deliberately restrained. The analysis finds that some popular arguments for revelation are substantially weaker than often claimed, while several skeptical objections also fail to establish what they are sometimes taken to prove. A number of arguments retain genuine conditional evidential force in either direction, but the study does not establish a defensible overall Bayesian ranking between divine revelation and human origin. The final chapter also develops an epistemic ḥujjah problem, asking what follows if a competent, adequately informed and nonresistant investigator can remain rationally uncertain about Muhammad’s prophetic authority, and how this bears on claims about divine authentication, culpability, and religious responsibility. Written for readers interested in philosophy of religion, Qur’anic studies, historical method, and comparative epistemology, Divine Revelation or Human Origin? is not an attempt to replace scholarship with probability language, nor to disguise theological assumptions as mathematics. Its aim is to identify exactly where the evidence discriminates between competing explanations, where it does not, and what further work would be required to justify a stronger conclusion.

title: Works for 8/3/2026 - Emily Dickinson
abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/ea6df646-03a8-47e2-b9e6-4cb308ffa567?authuser=1 The Body Is Built to Navigate: Quantum-Governed Embodiment, Relational Mapping, and a Catholic Invariant Grammar of Convergence presents a general theory of human navigation across physical, conceptual, social, moral, scientific, and religious domains. Its governing distinction is that a navigation system does not directly measure its destination. It estimates the traveler’s changing relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, then corrects movement over time. The paper traces this architecture across quantum-governed molecular processes, biological signal transduction, multisensory integration, neural oscillation, cognitive mapping, predictive modeling, memory, social coordination, and embodied action. It argues that the same general capacities used to move through physical environments also support navigation through ideas, relationships, values, traditions, rituals, and represented futures. A central distinction is drawn between navigational capacity, destination, and criterion. The body supplies the capacity to receive, remember, estimate, map, and correct, but biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good. Philosophies and religions therefore provide differing maps, authorities, practices, standards of error, and accounts of fulfillment. The interpretive method is Catholic Invariant Grammar, a relational framework that preserves distinctions such as source and manifestation, destination and path, sign and thing signified, participation and identity, nature and grace, observer and observed, sender and sent, and unity and distinction. This grammar permits comparison among Catholic, Taoist, Buddhist, Jewish, Muslim, scientific, philosophical, and secular accounts without collapsing them into a single doctrine. The specifically Catholic interpretation identifies the Father as ultimate source and end, the Son as the Way who reveals the Father within a genuine human history, and the Holy Spirit as the giver of living participation. The paper does not claim that biology or neuroscience discovers the Trinity. Instead, it distinguishes what can be empirically measured from what must be philosophically and theologically interpreted. The study also integrates Recursive History States, Wells of the Name, distributed measurement through the model of the Magi, and implications for artificial intelligence. Its central conclusion is that the body is built to navigate, history forms the map, communities preserve stable points of access, and interpretive traditions identify what should be followed and why.
